The centralized `_handleSDKError()` method (lines 390-425) handles runtime error classification: it checks `isinstance(error, AioRpcError)` for content filter detection (checking `error.details()` against `ETHIC_DETAILS`), and `isinstance(error, RunError)` for error-code logging. It returns a result object with `ModelResultStatus.ERROR` or `ModelResultStatus.CONTENT_FILTER`.

title: YC SDK auth resolution: _resolveAuth() with 4 modes + auto-fallback chain
content: `yc_sdk_provider.py` `_resolveAuth()` supports `auth_type` (config key `auth-type`): "auto" (env var fallback: `YC_API_KEY` → `YC_IAM_TOKEN` → `yc` CLI), "api-key" (API key auth using `YC_API_KEY` env var or config value `api-key`), "iam-token" (IAM token auth using `YC_IAM_TOKEN` env var or config value `iam-token`), "yc-cli" (Yandex Cloud CLI auth, optional `yc_profile` config key). Note: the runtime config string values use hyphens (api-key, iam-token, yc-cli), NOT underscores. `yc_profile` is optional (only passed to `AsyncAIStudio` when set, since SDK uses `UndefinedOr[str]` and rejects `None`). `folder_id` remains required. `_initSDK()` delegates entirely to `_resolveAuth()`.

title: YC SDK tokenization: SDK tokenize() with heuristic fallback
content: `yc_sdk_provider.py` `getExactTokensCount()` tries `self._ycModel.tokenize(messages)` first (uses SDK's native tokenizer). If unavailable (not all models support it), falls back to `getEstimateTokensCount()` heuristic. This avoids hard failure on models without tokenize endpoint.

title: YC SDK structured output: fresh model at lowered temperature for JSON schema
content: `yc_sdk_provider.py` `_generateStructured()` creates a fresh model via `_getModel(response_format={"json_schema": schema, "name": schemaName, "strict": strict})` at a lowered temperature `min(self.temperature, 0.3)` — never above 0.3 for structured output to encourage deterministic JSON. Parses JSON from response text, returns `ModelStructuredResult` with `data` on success or error on parse failure.

title: YC SDK centralized error handler: _handleSDKError()
content: `yc_sdk_provider.py` `_handleSDKError()` is the centralized error handler for SDK calls. Maps `AioRpcError` with ethic content → `ModelResultStatus.CONTENT_FILTER`. Maps `RunError` → log code + message, returns error result. `_generateText` catches `AIStudioError` specifically; `_generateImage` catches `Exception` for broader coverage including content filter detection from `AioRpcError`.

title: Pyright ignore comment must be on same line as attribute access in YC SDK
content: In `yc_sdk_provider.py`, when suppressing pyright errors for SDK attribute access (e.g., `result.status` where the SDK type stub doesn't match runtime), the `# pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]` comment must be on the SAME line as the attribute access (the line containing `result.status`), NOT on the closing parenthesis or a subsequent line. Otherwise pyright still flags the error.

title: Bugfix: _convertMessages needs callId→name map for tool result messages
content: In `yc_sdk_provider.py` `_convertMessages()` (lines 306-372), tool result messages (with `toolCallId` set) need a function-name lookup for YC SDK format (`{"name": <function_name>, "content": <result>}`). The `_convertMessages` method builds a `callIdToName: Dict[str, str]` map by scanning all messages for `toolCalls` (lines 322-327), storing `callIdToName[tc.id] = tc.name`. When converting tool result messages (line 349), it looks up the function name via `callIdToName.get(str(m.toolCallId), str(m.toolCallId))` — falling back to the raw toolCallId if no match found. Note: assistant messages with toolCalls are NOT stripped to bare role+text dicts. Instead, they are wrapped in `_ModelMessageWToolCalls` (line 358) which reconstructs protobuf ToolCallList objects to satisfy the SDK's internal `message_to_proto` pipeline.

title: Decision: _generateStructured uses _handleSDKError like all other methods
content:
In `yc_sdk_provider.py`, `_generateStructured` was catching `Exception` and re-raising (`raise`), inconsistent with `_generateText` and `_generateImage` (both catch `Exception` → `_handleSDKError()`).

Fixed: Changed `except Exception: logger.error(...); raise` to `return self._handleSDKError(e, retType=ModelStructuredResult)`. The return type is handled via `@overload` declarations on `_handleSDKError` (lines 374-388) rather than `# type: ignore[return-value]` suppression comments.

Also removed the `Raises` docstring entry for `ai.AioRpcError` (which doesn't exist as a valid import path) and replaced with note that errors are handled via `_handleSDKError`.

All three methods now catch `Exception` (not different types) and route to the same centralized error handler.

title: Bugfix: supportText/supportImages validation was removed during _initModel() refactoring
content:
The `yc_sdk_provider.py` `__init__` docstring says `Raises ValueError` for incompatible `supportText`/`supportImages` flags, but the validation was silently removed when `_initModel()` was refactored away. The YC SDK provider only supports either text OR image models, not both, and at least one must be set.

Restored in `__init__` after `super().__init__(...)`:
```python
if self.supportText and self.supportImages:
    raise ValueError("Only one of support_text and support_images can be True for YC SDK model")
if not self.supportText and not self.supportImages:
    raise ValueError("Either support_text or support_images must be True for YC SDK model")
```

title: Bugfix: _statusToModelRunResultStatus now handles unknown codes gracefully
content: `yc_sdk_provider.py` `_statusToModelRunResultStatus(int) -> ModelResultStatus` was calling `ModelResultStatus(status)` directly, which raises `ValueError` for unrecognized status codes. Wrapped in `try/except ValueError`, returning `ModelResultStatus.UNKNOWN` and logging a warning for unrecognized codes.

title: Gotcha: _resolveAuth return type needs Union not | syntax, string-quoted
content:
`yc_sdk_provider.py` `_resolveAuth()` return type `\"YandexCloudCLIAuth | APIKeyAuth | IAMTokenAuth\"` uses py3.10 `|` union syntax, but the file doesn't have `from __future__ import annotations`. This causes runtime issues (py3.12+ supports `|` in annotations, but string-quoted `|` union syntax isn't resolved correctly).

Fixed to use `\"Union[YandexCloudCLIAuth, APIKeyAuth, IAMTokenAuth]\"` with `from typing import Union` added to imports.

title: Gotcha: YC OpenAI provider base URL mismatch (llm.api → ai.api) breaks tests
content:
The YC OpenAI provider's `_getBaseUrl()` (yc_openai_provider.py:290) returns `https://ai.api.cloud.yandex.net/v1`. This is the currently-intended production URL.

Note: The test file `tests/lib/ai/providers/test_yc_openai_provider.py` does **not** assert any specific base_url value — there are no test assertions checking `https://llm.api.cloud.yandex.net/v1` or any other URL. If tests were previously failing due to a URL mismatch, the test assertions have already been updated or removed.

title: _handleSDKError TypeVar replaced with @overload due to pyright constructor kwarg limitation
content:
**Problem:** `lib/ai/providers/yc_sdk_provider.py` had a generic `_handleSDKError[_TModelRunResult]` method where `retType: Type[_TModelRunResult]` was called with keyword arguments (`rawResult=`, `status=`, `resultText=`, `error=`). Pyright (basic mode) could not resolve constructor keyword parameters on a `Type[TypeVar]` — it's a known limitation. Pyright reported 4 instances of `No parameter named "rawResult"` etc.

**Solution:** Replaced the module-level `_TModelRunResult = TypeVar("_TModelRunResult", bound=ModelRunResult)` with `@overload` signatures:

1. Two `@overload` stubs: one for `Type[ModelRunResult]` (default), one for `Type[ModelStructuredResult]` — ordered with the more-specific (`ModelStructuredResult`) first to ensure correct overload resolution (since `Type` is covariant, `Type[ModelStructuredResult]` is assignable to `Type[ModelRunResult]`, and pyright matches top-to-bottom).
2. Implementation uses `Type[ModelRunResult] | Type[ModelStructuredResult]` and explicitly branches on `retType` (`if retType is ModelStructuredResult: ... else: ...`).
3. Removed `TypeVar` from imports, added `overload`.
4. Removed unused `TYPE_CHECKING` import.
5. Black reformats `@overload` stubs with `...` on the same line as `def`, which triggers flake8 E704. Fixed with `# noqa: E704` inline comments on overload lines.

**Key lesson:** When pyright can't resolve constructor kwargs on `Type[TypeVar]`, use `@overload` with concrete types. Order overloads with the most specific type first to avoid incorrect resolution due to Type covariance.

title: Black reformats @overload stubs to single-line ... triggering flake8 E704
content:
**Problem:** `black` reformats `@overload` stub methods to have `...` on the same line as the function signature (e.g. `def _handleSDKError(...) -> ModelStructuredResult: ...`). `flake8` then reports E704 (multiple statements on one line) for these stubs. This happens because `black` treats `...` as a single expression statement on the same line.

**Solution:** The project's `pyproject.toml` flake8 config does NOT include `E704` in `extend-ignore`. The fix used in `lib/ai/providers/yc_sdk_provider.py` is to add `# noqa: E704` inline comments on overload stub lines. This is the preferred approach because:
1. Adding E704 to global `extend-ignore` would suppress legitimate cases elsewhere.
2. Expanding to multi-line (putting `...` on its own line) fights black on subsequent reformats.
3. Inline suppression is narrow and explicit.

**Lesson:** When adding `@overload` stubs in a black+flake8 project, always add `# noqa: E704` on overload lines to prevent the format/lint cycle conflict.

title: YC SDK ToolCallList construction: proto has no id field, needs both tool_calls tuple and _proto_origin
content:
When constructing `ToolCallList` for `_ModelMessageWToolCalls` in `yc_sdk_provider.py`, critical details:

1. **Protobuf `ToolCall` has NO `id` field** — The `yandex.cloud.ai.foundation_models.v1.text_common_pb2.ToolCall` proto message has only `function_call`. Tool call IDs only exist in the JSON/HTTP representation. The SDK's own `BaseToolCall._from_proto()` always passes `id=None` when constructing from proto. Do NOT pass `id` to `ProtoCompletionsToolCall(...)` — it will fail at runtime.

2. **`ToolCallList` requires both `tool_calls` and `_proto_origin`** — It's a generic frozen dataclass `ToolCallList[ProtoToolCallListTypeT, ToolCallTypeT]` with fields `tool_calls: tuple[ToolCallTypeT, ...]` and `_proto_origin: ProtoToolCallListTypeT`. An empty `ToolCallList()` call with no arguments will have:
   - `tool_calls = ()` (falsy — `len == 0`), causing the `message.tool_calls` truthiness check in the SDK's `message_to_proto()` to fail
   - No `_proto_origin`, so the gRPC call gets a broken proto

3. **Full construction chain from `LLMToolCall`**:
   - Build `ProtoCompletionsFunctionCall(name=tc.name, arguments=Struct(...))` from `tc.parameters`
   - Build `ProtoCompletionsToolCall(function_call=protoFc)` — no `id` parameter!
   - Create `AsyncFunctionCall(name=..., arguments=..., _proto_origin=protoFc)` SDK wrapper
   - Create `AsyncToolCall(id=str(tc.id) or None, function=fc, _proto_origin=protoTc, _json_origin=None)` SDK wrapper
   - Bundle proto calls into `ProtoCompletionsToolCallList(tool_calls=[...])`
   - Create `ToolCallList(tool_calls=tuple(sdkCalls), _proto_origin=protoList)`

    This ensures the SDK wrapper objects are fully consistent (matching what `_from_proto` would produce), while the protobuf objects carry the actual data that `message_to_proto` serializes for gRPC.

title: Regression: _extractUsage removed — direct result.usage access crashes when usage is None
content:
The refactoring of `yc_sdk_provider.py` removed the `_extractUsage` static method and replaced it with direct property access in two of three generation methods (`_generateText` and `_generateStructured`):

```python
inputTokens = result.usage.input_text_tokens
outputTokens = result.usage.completion_tokens
totalTokens = result.usage.total_tokens
```

Notably, `_generateImage` does **not** access `result.usage` at all — `ImageGenerationModelResult` has no `usage` field (only `image_bytes` and `model_version`), so no token counts are reported for image generation.

The SDK types `GPTModelResult.usage` as `CompletionUsage` (non-Optional), so `result.usage` is never `None` for a valid response under the current SDK. The `_generateText` and `_generateStructured` paths are protected by preceding `isinstance(result, GPTModelResult)` TypeError guards (lines 463, 584).

This is a defensive programming concern: if the SDK were changed in the future to return `usage = None` for partial/streaming results, the code would crash. The previous `_extractUsage` pattern (using `getattr` with None fallbacks) was more defensive. Consider adding inline None guards if the SDK's type contract changes.

title: gRPC fork_posix.cc log suppression — GRPC_VERBOSITY env var before import
content:
When `yandex-ai-studio-sdk` (or its dependency `grpcio`) is first imported, gRPC's C++ core logs a message like `I0514 21:02:59.800020 30097272 fork_posix.cc:71] Other threads are currently calling into gRPC, skipping fork() handlers` to stderr via glog. This is NOT controlled by Python's `logging` module.

To suppress it, set `os.environ.setdefault("GRPC_VERBOSITY", "ERROR")` before gRPC is imported (at module level). This tells the C++ gRPC core to only emit ERROR-level messages.

Additionally, silence the Python-level gRPC logger with `logging.getLogger("grpc").setLevel(logging.ERROR)`.

**Known constraint**: `from __future__ import annotations` must be the first statement in the file (after docstring). The `os.environ.setdefault(...)` call must come AFTER `from __future__` but BEFORE the other imports. This triggers flake8 E402 on the subsequent stdlib imports — use `# noqa: E402` on those lines or move the env var setting to before the `from __future__` line (as a bare `import os` + `os.environ.setdefault(...)` before the docstring). The simpler approach used in `scripts/check_tool_calling.py`: put it between `from __future__` and other imports, with `# noqa: E402` annotations.

First discovered in `scripts/check_tool_calling.py` (June 2026) when testing YC SDK models via `yc-openai` provider.

title: Tool-calling probe classification must track success across ALL turns, not just final response
content:
In `scripts/check_tool_calling.py`, `probeModel()` implements a multi-turn tool-calling loop: when the model returns `TOOL_CALLS`, the script executes the fake tool, sends the result back, and calls the model again (up to 5 turns). 

**Bug discovered**: `classifyResult()` was called only on the final API result (the last turn's response). When the model correctly called the tool on turn 1 but returned a plain text answer on turn 2, the classification would see `FINAL` status with no `toolCalls` and return `NO_TOOL_CALL` — incorrectly reporting the model as failing the tool-call test.

**Fix**: Track `toolCalledCorrectly: bool` across the entire loop. When any turn produces a `TOOL_CALLS` result with a matching tool name and valid parameters, set `toolCalledCorrectly = True`. After the loop, use this flag for final classification: if `toolCalledCorrectly`, return `PASS` regardless of the final turn's status.

Also, `rawResult` (used for token counts in verbose output) holds only the LAST result. In a multi-turn tool-call exchange, token counts from early turns (where the model produced the tool call) are lost. This is by design (mirrors LLMService behavior) but means displayed token counts may be lower than total consumed over all turns.

title: Gotcha: YC OpenAI provider model ID format (gpt://) incompatible with OpenAI models.list() response
content:
The `YcOpenaiProvider` (lib/ai/providers/yc_openai_provider.py) uses Yandex Cloud's OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `https://ai.api.cloud.yandex.net/v1` and formats model IDs as `gpt://<folder_id>/<model>/<version>` (e.g., `gpt://b1g.../yandexgpt/latest`). This means even if `self._client.models.list()` were called (which hits `GET /models`), the returned model IDs from the standard OpenAI `/v1/models` endpoint would NOT match the `gpt://` URI format that the provider expects for generation. The IDs would be opaque native identifiers, not the URI format used by the provider's `_getModelId()` override.

This is distinct from the YC AI Studio SDK provider (YcAIProvider in yc_sdk_provider.py), which uses a completely different SDK interface and has its own model listing mechanism via `sdk.chat.completions.list()`.

Implication: If implementing remote model listing for YcOpenaiProvider, the `models.list()` OpenAI SDK call on this endpoint likely won't return useful results. Any model discovery for Yandex Cloud must go through the SDK provider or use a different approach.

title: Architecture: Two distinct provider families — OpenAI-compatible (has _client) vs SDK-based (no _client)
content:
The project's LLM providers split into two fundamentally different families:

1. **OpenAI-compatible providers** (inherit from `BasicOpenAIProvider`): `YcOpenaiProvider`, `OpenrouterProvider`, `CustomOpenAIProvider`. All have `self._client: Optional[openai.AsyncOpenAI] = None` initialized by `_initClient()`. They use the OpenAI Python SDK for API calls. Features that depend on `self._client` (e.g., `await self._client.models.list()`) work for these providers.

2. **SDK-based provider** (`YcAIProvider` in `yc_sdk_provider.py`): Extends `AbstractLLMProvider` directly, NOT `BasicOpenAIProvider`. Has `self._ycAISDK: AsyncAIStudio` instead of `self._client`. Uses the Yandex AI Studio SDK (`yandex_ai_studio_sdk.AsyncAIStudio`) with a completely different API surface (e.g., `self._ycAISDK.models.completions(modelId)`). It has no `_client` attribute at all.

This means any cross-provider feature (model listing, tool calling, structured output) needs two separate implementations: one for the OpenAI-compatible path and one for the YC SDK path. The base URL for the OpenAI-compatible providers is parameterized via the `_getBaseUrl()` hook.

title: Baseline: AbstractLLMProvider interface had zero remote model discovery before listRemoteModels() was added
content:
The original `AbstractLLMProvider` (lib/ai/abstract.py) had the following concrete (not abstract) methods, all purely local/in-memory with zero remote API calls:
- `listModels()`: returns `list(self.models.keys())` — names of models registered via `addModel()` from config
- `getModel(name)`: returns model from `self.models` dict
- `getModelInfo(name)`: returns model info dict
- `deleteModel(name)`: removes from `self.models` dict

`addModel()` was the only abstract method. No method existed that queried any API for available models. There was also no `fetchModels()`, `discoverModels()`, or any similar concept. No code anywhere in the project called `self._client.models.list()` or equivalent.

The `LLMManager.listModels()` (lib/ai/manager.py) similarly returned keys from `self.modelRegistry` — names registered from config, not discovered from any remote endpoint.

This baseline is important context: the `listRemoteModels()` async method added later (documented in memory 51f3176a) was an entirely new capability, not a modification of existing code.

title: Model config field defaults applied by LLMManager._initModels()
content:
When `LLMManager._initModels()` (`lib/ai/manager.py` lines ~130-187) reads each model entry from `config["models"]`, it applies these Python-side defaults for fields NOT present in the TOML config:

- `model_version` → `"latest"`
- `temperature` → `0.5`
- `context` → `32768`
- `enabled` → `True`

Required fields that MUST be in the TOML entry: `provider` (must match a key in `[models.providers]`), `model_id` (provider-specific model identifier).

The full set of recognized fields across model TOML entries: `provider`, `model_id`, `model_version`, `temperature`, `context`, `enabled`, `support_text`, `support_images`, `support_tools`, `support_structured_output`, `tier`.

These defaults are NOT written in the config files — they exist only in the Python code. If a model config omits `temperature`, it silently gets 0.5; if it omits `context`, it gets 32768. This is important to know when adding new model entries or debugging unexpected behavior.

title: extraConfig pattern: raw model config dict stored as model._config
content:
In `LLMManager._initModels()`, the full raw model config dict from TOML is passed to `provider.addModel(..., extraConfig=modelConfig)`. Provider implementations store it as `model._config` (a dict). This is how provider-specific flags like `support_tools`, `support_images`, `support_structured_output`, and `tier` are passed through the generic `AbstractModel` interface without the model base classes needing to know about them.

Scripts (e.g., `check_tool_calling.py`, `check_structured_output.py`) access these flags via `model._config.get("support_tools", False)` — the base model classes DON'T have `support_tools` as a field; it's only in the raw config. This is the canonical pattern for reading non-standard model attributes from scripts/tools.

title: Shell wrapper script convention: _load_env.sh sourced after cd to repo root
content:
All shell wrapper scripts (e.g., `scripts/run-check-tool-calling.sh`, `scripts/run-llm-debug-query.sh`, etc.) follow this exact pattern:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."          # always cd to repo root first
. "scripts/_load_env.sh"         # source the shared env loader (parses --env=NAME, builds $CONFIG_DIRS)
./venv/bin/python scripts/<script>.py --dotenv-file "$ENV_FILE" --config-dir ./configs/00-defaults $CONFIG_DIRS $@
```

`scripts/_load_env.sh` does three things:
1. Parses `--env=NAME` from args (default `local`), constructs `ENV_FILE=.env.NAME`
2. Sources the `.env*` file with trace suppressed to avoid leaking secrets
3. Reads `$CONFIGS` env var (default `local`, space-separated list of subdirs), builds `$CONFIG_DIRS` as `--config-dir ./configs/<dir>` for each

The `_load_env.sh` is written to inherit and mutate the caller's `$@` (it shifts away `--env=...`). Callers must NOT pass arguments to the `.` command — just source it bare.

title: scripts/list_models.py: remote model lookup fallback strategy (model_id → config key)
content:
In `scripts/list_models.py`, when comparing locally configured models against remote model listings, the script tries two keys to find the matching remote model:

1. First, `model_id` from the local config (the actual API identifier string, e.g., `"openai/gpt-4o"`)
2. If not found by `model_id`, falls back to the config key name (the TOML section key, e.g., `"gpt-4o"`)

This dual-lookup is necessary because some configs use a human-readable key name that differs from the remote API's model ID. The match logic:
```python
remoteInfo = remoteModels.get(modelId) or remoteModels.get(modelName)
```

If neither key is found in the remote list, the model is reported as "NOT IN REMOTE LIST" and counts as a mismatch.

title: listRemoteModels() uses raw HTTP for OpenRouter to preserve context_length and pricing fields
content: The `listRemoteModels()` method on `OpenrouterProvider` (`lib/ai/providers/openrouter_provider.py`) deliberately uses raw `httpx` HTTP calls instead of the OpenAI SDK's `client.models.list()`. Rationale: the OpenAI SDK's `Model` type strips `context_length` and `pricing` fields from the OpenRouter API response. The raw HTTP call to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models` preserves the full response, which is necessary for comparing remote vs. local model configs in `scripts/list_models.py`. The method signature is `async def listRemoteModels(self) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]`, returning a dict mapping model IDs to their full settings dicts. Both error-returning default (`{}`) and exception-handling pattern match the `BasicOpenAIProvider` override.

title: scripts/list_models.py: _PROVIDER_TYPES is a manually maintained mapping that can drift
content: The `scripts/list_models.py` script hardcodes a `_PROVIDER_TYPES: Dict[str, type]` mapping from config provider type strings to provider classes (OpenrouterProvider, BasicOpenAIProvider, YcAIProvider, YcOpenaiProvider). If a new provider class is registered in `lib/ai/manager.py` but not added to this mapping, the script will fail with `"Unknown provider type: ..."` and no indication that the script itself needs updating. This is a utility script, not production code, but it creates a silent maintenance gap. A more robust approach would be auto-discovery from the provider modules or registering provider types in a lookup the script can import.

title: Gotcha: Struct.update(tc.parameters) crashes on None dict values in _ModelMessageWToolCalls
content:
In `lib/ai/providers/yc_sdk_provider.py`, the `_ModelMessageWToolCalls` class (line ~124) calls `argsStruct.update(tc.parameters)` where `tc.parameters` is a dict of tool call arguments parsed from JSON. The `if tc.parameters:` guard at line 125 only skips when `parameters` is None/empty/falsy — it does NOT protect against keys with `None` VALUES inside the dict (e.g. `{"location": None}`).

`Struct.update()` from `google.protobuf.struct_pb2` converts dict values to protobuf `Value` types, and protobuf `Value` does NOT support null — it raises `TypeError` for `None` values.

This is a realistic runtime crash scenario: LLMs frequently return `null` for optional parameters in tool calls.

**STATUS**: The fix described in the original memory (filtering None values before `update()`) has NOT been applied. As of June 2026, `tc.parameters` values of `None` are still passed directly into `argsStruct.update()` without any stripping. This is an open bug.

title: _handleSDKError implementation return type says ModelRunResult but can return ModelStructuredResult
content:
In `lib/ai/providers/yc_sdk_provider.py`, the `_handleSDKError` method has `@overload` signatures correctly declaring different return types for `ModelRunResult` vs `ModelStructuredResult`. However, the actual implementation signature at line ~397 says `-> ModelRunResult`, which is technically a valid lower bound since `ModelStructuredResult extends ModelRunResult`. But pyright (basic mode) won't infer the narrower return type when `retType=ModelStructuredResult` is passed, so callers expecting `ModelStructuredResult` lose type safety.

Distinct from the earlier TypeVar→@overload refactoring (memory #dd0b2e8e) which solved the pyright constructor kwarg limitation — this is about the impl signature still being too broad.

Fix: change implementation signature to `-> ModelRunResult | ModelStructuredResult`.

title: YC OpenAI base URL changed from `llm.api.cloud.yandex.net` to `ai.api.cloud.yandex.net`
content: In `lib/ai/providers/yc_openai_provider.py`, the base URL for the Yandex Cloud OpenAI-compatible API was changed from `llm.api.cloud.yandex.net` to `ai.api.cloud.yandex.net`. Golden test data (`tests/lib_ai/golden/data/YCOpenAI Basic.json`) was updated accordingly. This may be a Yandex API endpoint migration. Note: this is distinct from the YC SDK provider (`yc_sdk_provider.py`) which uses gRPC, not HTTP.

title: OpenRouterProvider.listRemoteModels creates new httpx.AsyncClient on every call (connection churn)
content: In `lib/ai/providers/openrouter_provider.py`, `listRemoteModels()` creates a new `httpx.AsyncClient` via `async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:` on every invocation (line ~264-305). For repeated calls (e.g., periodic model sync), this creates unnecessary TLS handshake and connection overhead. The parent `BasicOpenAIProvider` already has a long-lived `self._client` (an `openai.AsyncOpenAI` instance) that manages an underlying HTTP connection pool. Consider reusing `self._client._client` (the underlying `httpx.AsyncClient`) or creating a persistent client on the provider instance. Note: the raw HTTP approach is deliberate (to preserve `context_length` and `pricing` fields the OpenAI SDK strips — see memory #95a82e90), but the connection lifecycle should be managed.

title: Agent mistake: _matchMarker defined but match column missing in check_image_parsing.py table
content: During creation of `scripts/check_image_parsing.py`, the agent copied `_matchMarker()` from `check_tool_calling.py` but forgot to add the `match` column to the table output. The user caught the unused function and asked about the missing column. Fix: added the `match` column header, width calculation, and data row rendering in `renderTable()`, mirroring `check_tool_calling.py`'s pattern — ✓ for PASS, ✗ otherwise. This is a recurring gotcha when copying probe scripts: ensure every helper function has a consumer.

title: Script check_image_parsing.py probes image understanding across all models via model.generateText()
content:
A probe script scripts/check_image_parsing.py was created following the pattern of check_tool_calling.py and check_structured_output.py. Key design points:

- Emulates _parseImage from internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1224-1277
- Takes a required positional argument image_file (the path to a local image, NOT --image-file) and optional --message (defaults to the Russian prompt from configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml parse-image-prompt)
- Reads image data from disk into bytearray, detects MIME type (defaults to image/png if magic fails), builds ModelImageMessage
- Calls model.generateText() directly (not via LLMService) for each model — same as other probe scripts
- There is no support_vision flag on models; the script tries all text-capable models (support_text=True) and classifies failures as API_REJECT if error mentions image/vision/multimodal keywords
- Result classification: PASS (got text), NO_TEXT (empty response), CONTENT_FILTER, TIMEOUT, API_REJECT (image-not-supported), EXCEPTION, DRY_RUN
- Shell wrapper at scripts/run-check-image-parsing.sh follows standard pattern: _load_env.sh → Python with --dotenv-file

title: _parseImage method: image-parsing via LLM with dedicated model settings
content:
`_parseImage` method in `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1224-1277` is called when a user sends an image attachment and `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.PARSE_ATTACHMENTS].toBool()` is true (gated by the `PARSE_ATTACHMENTS` chat setting).

The caller context (around line 1774-1825):
1. Downloads the attachment via `self._bot.downloadAttachment(mediaId, fileId)`
2. Detects MIME type via `magic.from_buffer(mediaData, mime=True)` — only proceeds if `mime.startswith("image/")`
3. Gets the image parsing prompt from `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.PARSE_IMAGE_PROMPT].toStr()`
4. Builds messages: `[ModelMessage(role="system", content=imagePrompt), ModelImageMessage(role="user", content=ensuredMessage.messageText, image=bytearray(mediaData))]`
5. Spawns `_parseImage` via `asyncio.create_task(self._parseImage(ensuredMessage, ret.id, messages))` and tracks in background queue

The `_parseImage` method itself:
- Calls `self.llmService.generateText()` with:
  - `modelKey=ChatSettingsKey.IMAGE_PARSING_MODEL` and `fallbackKey=ChatSettingsKey.IMAGE_PARSING_FALLBACK_MODEL` — both are `ChatSettingsKey` enum values resolved via `resolveModel()` to an `AbstractModel` instance
- On success (status == FINAL): updates `mediaAttachments` table with `MediaStatus.DONE` and the generated `description` text
- On failure: updates with `MediaStatus.FAILED`
- Returns `bool: True on success, False on failure`

Note: `IMAGE_PARSING_MODEL` and `IMAGE_PARSING_FALLBACK_MODEL` exist as `ChatSettingsKey` enum values (line 299-301 of `internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py`) with corresponding entries in `_chatSettingsInfo` TypedDict (lines 614-620). These must be configured separately from the main chat model — they control which LLM handles image description.

title: Scripts model filtering pattern: _filterModels() iterates all LLM models with provider/model/limit filters
content:
Both `scripts/check_structured_output.py` and `scripts/check_tool_calling.py` implement a near-identical `_filterModels()` function for discovering and filtering LLM models to probe. The pattern:

```python
candidates = []
for modelName in llmManager.listModels():
    model = llmManager.getModel(modelName)
    if model is None:
        continue
    info = model.getInfo()
    if not info.get("support_text", True):  # skip image-only models
        continue
    providerName = llmManager.modelRegistry.get(modelName, "unknown")
    if providerFilter and providerName != providerFilter:
        continue
    if modelFilter and modelName != modelFilter:
        continue
    candidates.append((modelName, model, providerName))
    if limit and len(candidates) >= limit:
        break
return candidates
```

Key steps: (1) list all registered model names via `llmManager.listModels()`, (2) get each `AbstractModel` via `llmManager.getModel()`, (3) check `model.getInfo()` dict for capabilities like `support_text`, (4) look up provider name from `llmManager.modelRegistry` dict, (5) apply CLI filters (`--provider`, `--model`, `--limit`). Returns `List[tuple[modelName, model, providerName]]`.

This same pattern is also used by `scripts/check_image_parsing.py` (which additionally filters for `support_images` capability). The `_providerNameForModel()` helper is also duplicated across these scripts.

Note: `scripts/list_models.py` is different — it instantiates a single provider directly and calls `provider.listRemoteModels()` instead of using `_filterModels()`.

title: No shared Python utils module in scripts/: utilities duplicated across scripts
content:
There is no shared `scripts/utils.py` module. The following utilities are duplicated (copied) across multiple scripts:

- `_col()` / `_ANSI_*` ANSI color helpers: in `check_structured_output.py`, `check_tool_calling.py`, `run_llm_debug_query.py`
- `_truncate(text, maxLen)`: in `check_structured_output.py`, `check_tool_calling.py`
- `_DEFAULT_CONFIG_DIRS = ["configs/00-defaults", "configs/local"]`: in every Python script that takes `--config-dir`
- `_filterModels()` / `_providerNameForModel()`: in `check_structured_output.py`, `check_tool_calling.py`, `check_image_parsing.py`
- `ProbeResult` dataclass: in `check_structured_output.py` and `check_tool_calling.py` (structurally similar but not identical)
- `_matchMarker()` / `computeExitCode()` exit code computation: in both structured output and tool calling probes
- YAML literal block representer for multiline strings: in `convert_llm_log_to_readable.py` and `reproduce_llm_dialog.py`

The only shared resource is `scripts/_load_env.sh` (shell-level). All Python-level duplication is inline/copied. If a new probe script is created (e.g. `check_image_parsing.py`), it should follow the `_filterModels()` pattern from the existing scripts.

title: LLM replay dev command design: /llm_replay receives JSON as Telegram attachment, respects USE_TOOLS
content:
The `/llm_replay` dev command (in `DevCommandsHandler` at `internal/bot/common/handlers/dev_commands.py`) is designed as an in-bot command rather than a standalone script. Key design points:

- Syntax: `/llm_replay [<model_name>]` with a JSON file attached as a document (Telegram via `baseMessage.document.file_id` or Max via `attachment.payload.url`). Model name is OPTIONAL — defaults to the chat's configured model.
- Downloads the file via `self._bot.downloadAttachment()` using platform-specific file reference.
- Reconstructs `ModelMessage` list from JSON using `ModelMessage.fromDictList(data["request"])` (line 977). Note: the docstring at line 842 references a `reconstructMessages` utility that does not exist in the current codebase — the docstring is stale.
- Sends through `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM` with all registered tools available.
- Tool usage respects the chat's `USE_TOOLS` setting (not forced).
- Streams intermediate responses back to the chat.
- Reports final summary with token counts and tool calls.
- Restricted to bot owners only (`CommandPermission.BOT_OWNER`).
- Also works with messages replied-to (extracts document from the replied-to message).

title: Plan document convention: detailed implementation plans go in docs/plans/
content: When designing multi-feature changes that span both scripts and bot code, a plan document is written to `docs/plans/<topic>.md` before implementation. The plan covers: file locations, function signatures, data flows, API contracts, design decisions, and implementation steps for each feature. Existing plans use a Status header (e.g., "> **Status:** Implemented" or just the body as a spec). Example: `docs/plans/llm-replay-and-yaml-conversion.md`.

title: run_llm_debug_query.py does NOT pass tools to generateText — useless for tool-calling debugging
content: The script `scripts/run_llm_debug_query.py` reconstructs LLM request messages from log files and re-runs the query via `model.generateText(messages)`. It does NOT pass any tools to `generateText()` — the call is bare. This means the script is only useful for debugging plain text-completion flows. Anyone trying to debug tool-calling scenarios (where the LLM should invoke a tool) will find the script inadequate. For in-bot tool-calling replay, use the `/llm_replay` dev command instead, which runs through the full LLMService pipeline with registered tools and the tool-execution loop.

title: LLMService.generateTextViaLLM dual tool detection: JSON code blocks AND [TOOL_CALL_START] custom markup
content:
Inside `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM()` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`), after getting a ModelRunResult with status FINAL, the service checks for tool calls using THREE patterns at lines 485-492 before deciding the result is truly a text response:

1. **Standard JSON code blocks** (line 487): A fenced code block ````json\n{\n  "name": "toolName",\n  "arguments": { ... }\n}\n```` with `name` + `arguments`/`parameters` keys. Matched by `_matchTextForJSONToolCall`.
2. **Custom markup** (line 490): `[TOOL_CALL_START] toolName{...args...}` — a bracket-delimited prefix followed by the tool name and JSON args inline. Matched by `_matchTextForToolCallStart`.
3. **Square-bracket + JSON** (line 492): `[tool_name]\n{json}` — tool name in square brackets followed by a JSON object on subsequent lines. Matched by `_matchTextForToolCallSquareBracketsAndJson`.

If any of the three patterns is detected, the status is promoted from FINAL to TOOL_CALLS and the tool-execution loop runs. This detection exists because some models produce function calls in formats other than the native tool_calls API response format. The first pattern (`[TOOL_CALL_START]`) is a custom markup used by Gromozeka's prompt templates.

title: JSONL silent data loss removed from llmReplayCommand — fail fast on malformed attachments
content:
The initial `/llm_replay` implementation in `DevCommandsHandler.llmReplayCommand` had a JSONL (one-JSON-per-line) fallback parsing loop that silently skipped lines failing `json.loads()`, discarding data without warning to the user. For a debugging/replay tool, silent data corruption is especially harmful.

Fix: removed the JSONL fallback entirely. The code now only handles two valid shapes: `json.loads()` returns a `dict` (used directly) or a `list` (extracts `data[0]`, expects it to be a dict). If the file isn't valid JSON or the shape is unexpected, the error is reported to the user immediately with a clear message. This is a deliberate design decision: fail fast rather than silently corrupt.

Note: the normalization at `dev_commands.py:953-964` does NOT wrap a dict in a list; it passes the dict through directly. For a list, it extracts `data[0]` (first element) rather than using the whole list.

title: Mock test pyright pragma for DevCommandsHandler tests
content:
When writing integration tests for `DevCommandsHandler`, pyright in `basic` mode flags false positives on:
- AsyncMock attributes like `.assert_awaited_once`, `.call_args`, `.await_count`
- Optional member access on `Optional[TheBot]` like `handler._bot.downloadAttachment`
- Decorator-altered call signatures on command methods called directly

Fix: add the following pragma comment at the top of any mock-heavy test file (after the module docstring):
```python
# pyright: reportAttributeAccessIssue=false, reportOptionalMemberAccess=false, reportCallIssue=false
```
This suppresses all three categories for the entire file, which is standard practice for mock-heavy test modules in this project.

title: YAML round-trip trailing newline limitation in convert_readable_to_llm_log.py
content:
The reverse conversion script `scripts/convert_readable_to_llm_log.py` has a known round-trip fidelity limitation: content originally ending with `\\n` (escape sequence) in the JSON log format will lose the trailing newline after a full JSON→YAML→JSON round trip.

Root cause: YAML's `|` (literal block style) uses "clip" chomping by default, which adds exactly one trailing newline. After the forward conversion (in `convert_llm_log_to_readable.py`), the `convertContentBack` in the reverse script strips one trailing newline to undo this YAML artifact. However, it cannot distinguish between "the YAML added a trailing newline" and "the original content actually ended with `\\n`".

This is documented as a known limitation. In practice, LLM log content rarely ends with `\n`, so the risk is low. If complete fidelity is ever needed, one could use `|+` (keep) or `|-` (strip) chomping indicators, or store a metadata flag.

title: DevCommandsHandler: no custom __init__, no tests, inherits all services from BaseBotHandler
content:
DevCommandsHandler (internal/bot/common/handlers/dev_commands.py) does NOT define its own __init__ method. It relies entirely on BaseBotHandler.__init__ (base.py L133-163), which sets up: self.configManager, self.config, self.db, self.botProvider, self.cache (CacheService.getInstance()), self.queueService (QueueService.getInstance()), self.storage (StorageService.getInstance()), self.llmService (LLMService.getInstance()), and self._bot (injected later via injectBot()).

This differs from handlers like WeatherHandler or YandexSearchHandler which have custom __init__ for proxy resolution or additional client initialization.

Tests exist at: tests/bot/common/handlers/test_dev_commands.py (moved from the old collocated internal/bot/common/handlers/ location to the canonical tests/ directory on June 12, 2026). Any new command added here must include tests.

The handler registers with HandlerParallelism.PARALLEL in HandlersManager (handler chain position #6, after SummarizationHandler).

title: Command visibility/availableFor pairing convention: BotOwner vs Public
content:
Bot commands in Gromozeka use two distinct visibility/availableFor pairing conventions, depending on who can execute them:

**BotOwner-restricted commands** (for developer/debug/admin commands):
```python
visibility={CommandPermission.BOT_OWNER},
availableFor={CommandPermission.BOT_OWNER},
```
This makes the command invisible in /help for non-owners and non-executable by non-owners. Used for: `models`, `settings`, `set`/`unset`, `test`, `clear_cache`, `get_admins`, `shutdown`.

**Public commands** (for user-facing features):
```python
visibility={CommandPermission.PRIVATE, CommandPermission.HIDDEN},
availableFor={CommandPermission.DEFAULT},
```
`PRIVATE` means the command appears in private chat /help; `HIDDEN` means it shows in group /help too but is hidden from the auto-generated command list. `DEFAULT` permits all users. Used for: `echo`.

Key: `visibility` controls who sees it in /help listings; `availableFor` controls who can execute it. They are always set together with the same value for BotOwner commands.

title: sendMessage full signature from BaseBotHandler
content:
BaseBotHandler.sendMessage() (base.py L505-527) is the universal message-sending method. Its full signature:

```python
async def sendMessage(
    self,
    replyToMessage: Optional[EnsuredMessage],
    messageText: Optional[str] = None,
    *,
    addMessagePrefix: str = "",
    photoData: Optional[bytes] = None,
    sendMessageKWargs: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    tryMarkdownV2: bool = True,
    tryParseInputJSON: Optional[bool] = None,
    sendErrorIfAny: bool = True,
    skipLogs: bool = False,
    mediaPrompt: Optional[str] = None,
    messageCategory: MessageCategory = MessageCategory.BOT,
    inlineKeyboard: Optional[Sequence[Sequence[CallbackButton]]] = None,
    typingManager: Optional[TypingManager] = None,
    splitIfTooLong: bool = True,
    chatId: Optional[int] = None,
    threadId: Optional[int] = None,
    notify: Optional[bool] = None,
    attachmentList: Optional[Sequence[Tuple[bytes, MessageType, Optional[str]]]] = None,
    toolsHistory: Optional[Sequence[ModelMessage]] = None,
) -> List[EnsuredMessage]:
```

Important conventions:
- `messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_COMMAND_REPLY` for command responses
- `messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR` for error messages (see separate memory)
- `skipLogs=True` for noisy test loops (e.g. iterating many times in /test)
- Pass `typingManager=typingManager` from the command method signature to show typing indicator

title: Error reporting pattern: sendMessage with MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR
content:
All bot commands report errors back to the chat using a consistent pattern:

```python
await self.sendMessage(
    ensuredMessage,
    messageText="Error description here",
    messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR,
)
```

This pattern is used uniformly across DevCommandsHandler for:
- Validation failures (missing args, invalid input)
- Semantic errors (e.g., "Unknown key: `foo`")
- Missing dependencies (e.g., "No replied message found")
- Parsing errors (e.g., "Invalid iterations count: ...")

The decorator `replyErrorOnException=True` (default on commandHandlerV2) acts as a safety net for unhandled exceptions, but explicit error messages via BOT_ERROR are the standard pattern for expected failure modes.

Don't use BOT_ERROR for success responses — use BOT_COMMAND_REPLY for normal command output.

title: Reply-to message and attachment handling patterns for bot commands
content:
When a command needs to process a message that the user replied to (e.g., analyze a photo, inspect entities), use this two-step check pattern:

**Step 1: Check if the command message is a reply**
```python
if ensuredMessage.replyId is None:
    await self.sendMessage(ensuredMessage, messageText="Must reply to a message", messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR)
    return
```

**Step 2: Get the replied-to message**
```python
repliedMessage = ensuredMessage.getEnsuredRepliedToMessage()
if repliedMessage is None:
    await self.sendMessage(ensuredMessage, messageText="No replied message found", messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR)
    return
```

**For accessing raw platform message attributes** (Telegram entities, Max markup):
```python
message = ensuredMessage.getBaseMessage()
if isinstance(message, telegram.Message) and message.reply_to_message:
    # Access telegram.Message.entities, .text, etc.
elif isinstance(message, maxModels.Message) and message.link:
    # Access max models via message.link.message
```

**For downloading file attachments** (from media.py analyze_command):
Branch on self.botProvider:

**Telegram path:**
```python
if self.botProvider == BotProvider.TELEGRAM and isinstance(parentMessage, telegram.Message) and self._bot is not None:
    fileId = parentMessage.photo[-1].file_id  # or .sticker.file_id, etc.
    mediaData = await self._bot.downloadAttachment(mediaId="", fileId=fileId)
```

**Max path:**
```python
elif self.botProvider == BotProvider.MAX and isinstance(parentMessage, maxModels.Message) and self._bot is not None:
    for attachment in parentMessage.body.attachments:
        if isinstance(attachment, maxModels.PhotoAttachment):
            mediaData = await self._bot.downloadAttachment(mediaId=attachment.payload.token, fileId=attachment.payload.url)
```

downloadAttachment signature: `async def downloadAttachment(self, mediaId: str, fileId: str) -> Optional[bytes]` — returns None on failure.

title: convertContentBack algorithm for YAML→JSON reverse conversion
content:
In `scripts/convert_readable_to_llm_log.py`, the `convertContentBack()` function reverses the forward transformation by:

1. **Strip one trailing `\n`** — YAML literal block style (`|`) with default "clip" chomping always appends a trailing newline that was NOT in the original data. Strip exactly one if `content.endswith("\n")`. This is the inverse of the forward script's YAML serialization behavior.

2. **Replace remaining actual newlines with `\\n` escape sequences** — `content.replace("\n", "\\n")` converts all remaining actual newlines back to the literal `\n` escape sequences used in the JSON log format.

This reverses the forward `convertMessageContent()` which does `content.replace("\\n", "\n")` (literal backslash-n → actual newline).

The algorithm correctly handles these cases:
- **No newlines in content**: YAML doesn't use block style, no trailing newline added, nothing to strip, nothing to escape → passes through unchanged.
- **Multiline content without trailing `\n`**: YAML block style adds one trailing `\n`, strip it, then escape remaining newlines → correct round-trip.
- **Multiline content with trailing `\\n` (original)**: Forward converts to actual `\n`, YAML adds another `\n` → content ends with `\n\n`. Strip one `\n` → leaves the intentional one → escape it → correct round-trip.

Applied to both `content` (inside request messages) and `response` fields. Other fields (`raw`, `date`, `status`, `model`, `provider`, `tool_calls`, `tool_call_id`) are preserved unchanged since the forward script doesn't process them either.

title: LLM log conversion scripts: mirroring convention and input format asymmetry
content:
The two LLM log conversion scripts are designed as mirror images:

- `scripts/convert_llm_log_to_readable.py` (JSON/YAML → readable YAML) — forward direction
- `scripts/convert_readable_to_llm_log.py` (readable YAML → JSON) — reverse direction

**Mirroring convention:**
- `convertContent()` / `convertContentBack()` — paired string transformers
- `processMessage()` / `processMessageBack()` — per-message processing
- `processLogEntry()` / `processLogEntryBack()` — per-entry processing
- Identical argparse pattern: `buildParser()` → `main()` → `sys.exit(main())`
- Same error handling: `FileNotFoundError`, `yaml.YAMLError`, generic `Exception` → print message, return 1
- Output path derivation: forward replaces `.json` with `.readable.yaml`; reverse replaces `.readable.yaml` with `.json`

**Input format asymmetry:**
- Forward script (`convert_llm_log_to_readable.py`) accepts both JSON (one-JSON-per-line) and YAML input — uses YAML-first-then-JSON-fallback with file extension detection.
- Reverse script (`convert_readable_to_llm_log.py`) reads **YAML only** — this is intentional because the readable format is always YAML. It uses `yaml.safe_load_all()` for multi-document YAML support.

**Output formats:**
- Default: one JSON object per line (`json.dumps(entry)` + `\n` for each entry) — matches the original append-only log format.
- `--pretty`: formatted JSON array (`json.dumps(entries, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)`).

**Round-trip verification method:** A full JSON → YAML → JSON round trip (pipe output of forward script into reverse script) should produce byte-identical JSON. This is the standard verification approach for these scripts.

title: Gotcha: ExtraDataDict total=False causes pyright error on direct bracket access — use .get() with isinstance check
content:
When accessing fields from `ExtraDataDict` (defined in `internal/services/llm/models.py` as a `TypedDict(total=False)`), using bracket notation like `extraData["typingManager"]` causes pyright error: `"Could not access item in TypedDict "typingManager" is not a required key in "ExtraDataDict", so access may result in runtime exception`.

The fix is to use `.get()` with an `isinstance` check:

```python
# Instead of:
extraData["typingManager"].addTimeout(120)

# Use:
typingMgr = extraData.get("typingManager")
if isinstance(typingMgr, TypingManager):
    typingMgr.addTimeout(120)
    await typingMgr.sendTypingAction()
```

This pattern was needed in the `/llm_replay` command's `processIntermediateMessages` callback in `dev_commands.py`. The `.get()`/`isinstance` approach satisfies pyright because `isinstance` narrows the type from `Any` to the concrete `TypingManager` type.

title: internal/services/llm/__init__.py heavy import chain prevents collocated tests
content:
File `internal/services/llm/__init__.py` imports `from .service import LLMService, LLMToolHandler`, which triggers a deep import chain: `service.py` → `internal.bot.models.chat_settings` → more heavy dependencies. When pytest discovers any test file under `internal/services/llm/` (collocated), it tries to import the package's `__init__.py`, which triggers this chain and fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'internal'` because the import chain can't resolve at test collection time.

This means collocated tests under `internal/services/llm/` are not viable. Tests for `internal/services/llm/utils.py` (or any module under this package) MUST be placed under `tests/services/llm/` instead — matching the project convention of stripping `internal/` from the source path.

As of June 2026, no test file has been explicitly created for the reconstruct_messages module yet — the recommended location is `tests/services/llm/test_reconstruct_messages.py`.

title: Mocking pattern: EnsuredMessage with MessageType.DOCUMENT for attachment tests
content:
When testing bot commands that process document attachments (e.g., `/llm_replay` which needs a JSON file), the `EnsuredMessage` must be constructed or mocked with specific setup:

1. Set `messageType=MessageType.DOCUMENT` on the `EnsuredMessage` so the handler recognizes it as a document.
2. Mock `getBaseMessage()` to return a mock object with a `.document.file_id` attribute for the media ID path.
3. For reply-to-document resolution: Set `isReply=True` on the `EnsuredMessage`, and mock `getEnsuredRepliedToMessage()` to return another `EnsuredMessage` with `messageType=MessageType.DOCUMENT`.
4. Mock `self._bot.downloadAttachment(fileUniqueId, fileId)` on the bot to return `Optional[bytes]`.

This pattern is demonstrated in handler tests such as `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_dev_commands.py` (after the Phase 4 test reorganization moved all tests to `tests/`).

title: mockLlmService fixture pattern for handler tests: LLMManager chain + AsyncMock
content:
When writing tests for bot handlers that call `self.llmService`, the `mockLlmService` fixture must configure several collaborating objects in a specific chain:

```python
service = Mock(spec=LLMService)
manager = Mock()
mockModel = Mock(spec=AbstractModel)
manager.getModel = Mock(return_value=mockModel)
manager.listModels = Mock(return_value=["model-a", "model-b"])
service.getLLMManager = Mock(return_value=manager)
service.generateTextViaLLM = AsyncMock(return_value=modelRunResult)
```

Key details:
- `Mock(spec=LLMService)` ensures pyright type-checking works on the mock.
- `getLLMManager()` returns a plain `Mock` (no spec needed) since `LLMManager` has many methods.
- `getModel()` returns `Mock(spec=AbstractModel)` so the handler can call `.modelKey` on the result.
- `generateTextViaLLM` must be `AsyncMock` since it's an async method.
- The returned `ModelRunResult` must be constructed with the expected fields: `status`, `resultText`, `toolCalls`, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `totalTokens`, `elapsedTime`.

To inject the mock into the handler, use `mock.patch.object(LLMService, 'getInstance', return_value=mockLlmService)` before constructing the handler, since `BaseBotHandler.__init__` calls `LLMService.getInstance()`.

This pattern is demonstrated in handler tests such as `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_dev_commands.py` (after the Phase 4 test reorganization moved all tests to `tests/`).

title: Test fixture singleton bypass: direct assignment after `with patch` block leaves getInstance unpatched
content:
When writing handler tests that mock `LLMService` (or any singleton), a fragile pattern is to patch `getInstance` only during `__init__` and then assign the mock directly to the handler:

```python
with patch.object(LLMService, "getInstance", return_value=mockLlmService):
    h = DevCommandsHandler(bot, config, userId, chatSettingsManager=MagicMock())
h.llmService = mockLlmService  # workaround after patch is released
```

This is fragile because:
1. The `with` block ends before the fixture returns, restoring `getInstance` to its original behavior.
2. The direct `h.llmService = mockLlmService` reassignment works because `BaseBotHandler.__init__` stores `self.llmService = LLMService.getInstance()` (so the instance is cached on the handler).
3. But any code path that calls `LLMService.getInstance()` after the `with` block (e.g., inside a helper method called by the handler) would get a REAL (unpatched) instance, causing test failures that are hard to debug.

**Correct pattern**: Keep the `patch.object` active for the entire test scope. Either:
- Wrap the entire test body (not just `__init__`) in the `with` block, or
- Use a `@patch` decorator on the test function, or  
- Ensure the mock is set up as an autouse fixture that resets `_instance = None` so the patched `getInstance` is always called.

Alternatively, rely on the existing autouse fixture pattern from `tests/conftest.py` that resets singleton `_instance = None`, but the patched `getInstance` must remain active when the handler or its dependencies call it.

title: Tool-call matchers use shared helpers: _tryApplyToolCallMatch + _tryParseJson
content:
In `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM()` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`), three private methods (`_matchTextForJSONToolCall`, `_matchTextForToolCallStart`, `_matchTextForToolCallSquareBracketsAndJson`) detect tool calls embedded in LLM response text. They tried in sequence at lines 487-492, in order: JSON-fence → TOOL_CALL_START → square-bracket.

All three delegate to two shared helpers:
1. **`_tryApplyToolCallMatch(mlRunResult, *, toolName, parameters, toolCallId, prefixStr, suffixStr) -> bool`** (line 152): Centralized validation and in-place mutation. Only accepts when (a) prefix or suffix is empty (tool call at start or end of response), (b) toolName is registered in `self.toolsHandlers`, (c) parameters is a dict. On success, sets `status=TOOL_CALLS` and populates `toolCalls`.
2. **`_tryParseJson(data) -> Tuple[Any, int]`** (line 201): Wraps `json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode()` with a fallback that fixes escaped single quotes (`\\'` → `'`) before retrying. Returns both parsed object and end-position index.

All three matchers use greedy `{.*}` in their regex patterns, relying on `_tryParseJson`'s `raw_decode` to handle nested JSON (unlike the old non-greedy `{.*?}` which broke on nested objects). The greedy `{.*}` combined with `raw_decode` correctly extracts only the first JSON object, with trailing text preserved as suffix.

Key invariants:
- Tool call must appear at BEGINNING or END of response (prefix or suffix must be empty)
- Tool name must be in `self.toolsHandlers` to accept the match
- Invalid JSON causes a log warning and returns `False` (silent skip, not an error)

Downstream execution (line 510-518) also defensively checks `toolCall.name in self.toolsHandlers`, returning an error tool result if a tool call somehow passes the matchers with an unregistered name.

title: No unit tests for text-to-tool-call conversion paths in LLMService
content:
Of the five private methods that convert LLM response text to tool calls in `internal/services/llm/service.py`, only `_tryParseJson` has unit test coverage: 19 tests in `tests/services/llm/test_try_parse_json.py` covering valid JSON, invalid JSON, escaped single-quote fallback, end-position correctness, etc.

The other four methods (`_matchTextForJSONToolCall`, `_matchTextForToolCallStart`, `_matchTextForToolCallSquareBracketsAndJson`, `_tryApplyToolCallMatch`) have NO unit test coverage. Existing tests in `test_llm_service.py` and `test_llm_integration.py` only exercise tool calls that arrive with `status=TOOL_CALLS` from mocked models; they never test the text-to-tool-call regex conversion paths.

Test gaps include:
- Nested JSON parameters (the old `{.*?}` regex bug)
- `_tryApplyToolCallMatch` with unregistered tool name (should return False)
- Non-empty prefix AND non-empty suffix (should return False)
- `raw_decode` suffix computation (trailing text preserved in resultText)
- All three matchers with edge cases (empty tool name, non-dict parameters, invalid JSON)

title: Inconsistent .strip() in suffix computation across tool-call matchers
content:
In `internal/services/llm/service.py`, the three tool-call matchers compute the suffix differently after `_tryParseJson`:

1. `_matchTextForJSONToolCall` (line 261): `suffixStr = jsonStr[endPos:] + match.group(3)` — no `.strip()`
2. `_matchTextForToolCallStart` (line 307): `suffixStr = toolArgsStr[endPos:].strip() + match.group(4)` — with `.strip()`
3. `_matchTextForToolCallSquareBracketsAndJson` (line 351): `suffixStr = toolArgsStr[endPos:].strip() + match.group(4)` — with `.strip()`

The inconsistency between #1 and #2/#3 means the JSON-fence method may retain trailing whitespace/newlines from the raw_decode remainder in its suffix. In practice this is harmless because `_tryApplyToolCallMatch` applies a final `.strip()` to the combined `(prefixStr + suffixStr)`, but the inconsistency should be fixed for correctness and consistency.

title: Tool-call matcher cascade no longer short-circuits on JSON-in-backticks alone — hasMatch semantic change
content:
During the extraction of inline tool-call detection into three separate methods in `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM()` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`), the behavior of `hasMatch` changed subtly but intentionally.

**Old behavior (inline code):** When the JSON-backtick regex matched, `hasMatch` was set to `True` immediately — before trying to parse the JSON or validating it against `self.toolsHandlers`. This meant any backtick-wrapped JSON in LLM output prevented the `[TOOL_CALL_START]` pattern from being checked, even if the JSON wasn't a valid tool call.

**New behavior:** Each matcher returns `True` only when the full validation pipeline succeeds (greedy `{.*}` regex AND `_tryParseJson` AND `_tryApplyToolCallMatch` which checks `toolName in self.toolsHandlers`). If a pattern matches but fails validation, subsequent matchers are tried. Cascade order (lines 487-492): JSON-fence → TOOL_CALL_START → square-bracket.

**Impact:** This is strictly more correct — backtick-wrapped JSON that isn't a valid tool call no longer blocks `[TOOL_CALL_START]` detection. However, it could surface new tool-call matches in edge cases where an LLM outputs both unrelated JSON in code fences AND a `[TOOL_CALL_START]` markup in the same message. The old code would have missed the tool call silently; the new code detects it.

title: Behavioral change: TOOL_CALL_START matcher now gates on toolName in self.toolsHandlers
content:
In the refactoring of tool-call detection in LLMService.generateTextViaLLM() (internal/services/llm/service.py), the extracted _matchTextForToolCallStart method (and ALL three matchers) delegate to the shared helper _tryApplyToolCallMatch which checks toolName in self.toolsHandlers (line 189).

**Correction**: This guard was NOT newly added during refactoring. Git history shows the toolName in self.toolsHandlers check already existed inline in all three matchers before extraction. The refactoring centralized it into the shared _tryApplyToolCallMatch helper, but did not introduce it as a new guard.

The guard applies to ALL THREE matchers (JSON-fence, TOOL_CALL_START, square-bracket) via the shared _tryApplyToolCallMatch at service.py:186-190. If toolName is not in self.toolsHandlers, the matcher returns False and the text is left as-is in the LLM response.

Downstream execution (line 508-517) also defensively checks toolCall.name in self.toolsHandlers, returning an error tool result if a tool call somehow passes the matchers with an unregistered name.

title: Removed TODO about parameters/arguments requirement — design intent lost in refactoring
content: During the refactoring of tool-call text matching in `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM()` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`), the old inline code in `_matchTextForJSONToolCall` contained `# TODO: is "parameters"|"arguments" required?`. This comment was removed when the code was extracted into `_tryApplyToolCallMatch`. The resolution is encoded in the logic: `isinstance(parameters, dict)` on the first line of the shared helper effectively makes dict-typed parameters required (non-dict and None are rejected, returning False). Future readers lose this design rationale. Consider adding a comment near the `isinstance` check to preserve the design intent.

title: Type annotation gotcha: _tryApplyToolCallMatch parameters param is over-narrow as Optional[Dict]
content:
In `LLMService._tryApplyToolCallMatch()` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`), the `parameters` parameter is annotated as `Optional[Dict[Any, Any]]`, but this is over-narrow. Two of the three callers pass the result of `json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode()`, which can return any JSON value (list, string, number, bool, None) — not just `Dict | None`. The first caller (`_matchTextForJSONToolCall`) can also pass a non-dict value from `jsonData.get("arguments")` or `jsonData.get("parameters")` if the LLM returns a non-dict value for that key.

The runtime `isinstance(parameters, dict)` guard correctly handles non-dict values, so there is no runtime bug. However, the annotation misleads readers and future type-checking passes. The correct annotation should be `Any` since the method validates the type itself.

Suggested fix:
```python
def _tryApplyToolCallMatch(
    self,
    mlRunResult: ModelRunResult,
    *,
    toolName: str,
    parameters: Any,  # validated by isinstance() inside
    toolCallId: Optional[str],
    prefixStr: str,
    suffixStr: str,
) -> bool:
```

title: README scope: keep compact (~100-120 lines), link to detailed docs
content: The README.md was compacted from 847 lines to 103 lines by deliberate decision. The README should be a lightweight overview that can be read in 90 seconds. Essential content only: project one-liner, requirements (4 lines), feature bullets (~14 one-liners), 4-step quick start, minimal config snippet (~10 lines), key run commands (4 examples), key commands table (6 entries max with "see /help for the rest"), dev commands, troubleshooting, contributing, and license. Everything else — architecture diagrams, full project tree (~260 lines), full handler list, full command list (~50 lines), detailed config sections (~100 lines), migration guide, testing structure — belongs in `docs/developer-guide.md` or `docs/llm/`. Rationale: 847-line README was unreadable, forced users to scroll past content they didn't need, and duplicated information better kept in detailed docs.

title: README_BOT.md deleted: obsolete prototype docs should be removed, not rewritten
content: `README_BOT.md` was a "minimal Telegram bot" prototype description referencing files and methods that no longer exist (`database.py`, `test_bot.py`, `setup_handlers()`, `handle_message()`). The decision was to delete it entirely rather than rewrite it, because the comprehensive README.md already covers everything a rewrite would contain. A condensed duplicate would create a permanent maintenance/sync burden with no reader benefit. When a documentation file describes an old architecture that no longer exists and provides no unique value over current docs, deletion is the right approach.

title: Config env var for bot token is ${BOT_TOKEN}, not ${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}
content: The default config at `configs/00-defaults/00-config.toml` uses `token = "${BOT_TOKEN}"` as the bot token placeholder. When documenting config examples (e.g., in README.md), the env var name must be `${BOT_TOKEN}` — using `${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}` is wrong and will cause the bot to fail to start with an empty token. This applies regardless of platform (Telegram or Max Messenger use the same env var).

title: keepConnection in database config defaults to true, not false
content: The `database.providers.default.parameters.keepConnection` setting in `configs/00-defaults/00-config.toml` defaults to `true` (connect on creation and keep connection open). When documenting default config values (e.g., in README examples), using `keepConnection = false` is incorrect and misleads about connection behavior. The `keepConnection = true` default has meaningful consequences for connection timing and in-memory DB data retention.

title: Documentation drift detection workflow: explore → compare → fix → review → test
content:
The effective workflow used for the large-scale README overhaul (June 2026) was:

1. **Read baseline** — Read current README.md and key project docs (AGENTS.md, developer-guide.md, architecture docs, main.py entry point)
2. **Deep project exploration** — Explore full directory structure, read key source files (main.py, config system, handlers, services, database, libraries). Document everything found.
3. **Compare against documentation claims** — Catalog each README claim vs reality: class names, architecture, commands, features, test counts, config paths, licenses.
4. **Delegate targeted fixes** — Dispatch parallel tasks: one for the README rewrite (with detailed drift catalog as context), one for ancillary file cleanup (e.g., deleting README_BOT.md, fixing AGENTS.md references, fixing docs with stale class names).
5. **Code review** — Review all diffs for accuracy before committing. Critical issues found at this stage (e.g., wrong env var name, wrong config default).
6. **Quality gates** — Run `make format lint test` after every change batch.
7. **Narrow scope if needed** — If the result is still too large (847-line README), further compact based on user feedback.

This workflow is reusable for any large-scale documentation sync effort.

title: License is BSD 3-Clause, not MIT — README was wrong
content: The project's LICENSE file at repo root is BSD 3-Clause (Copyright (c) 2025, NotA Company). The README.md historically stated "MIT" — this was incorrect. When documenting the project, always refer to the license as BSD 3-Clause. Verified by reading `LICENSE` file directly.

title: README formatting specifics: no emojis, bold, link-to-docs pattern
content:
Compressing README.md from 847 to 103 lines confirmed these specific formatting rules:

1. **No emojis anywhere** in README — strictly banned.
2. **Bold** for feature name prefixes (e.g. `**Multi-provider LLM**: description`), not overused otherwise.
3. **Every verbose section gets a link** to `docs/developer-guide.md` or `docs/llm/index.md` — architecture diagrams, project tree (~260 lines), full handler list, migration guide, testing structure, detailed config sections.
4. **Feature list format**: exactly one line per feature with key name bolded, no sub-headers or paragraphs. ~10-14 items.
5. **Quick Start**: exactly 4 steps — `git clone`, `make install`, configure `.env` (link to config docs), `./run.sh`.
6. **Key commands table**: exactly 5-6 entries (`/start`, `/help`, `/configure`, `/taro`, `/weather`, `/search`) with "See `/help` in-chat for the full command list." note.
7. **Minimal config snippet**: ~6 lines showing only `bot.token`, `bot.mode`, `database.path`, `logging.level` — link to `docs/llm/configuration.md` for full docs.
8. **Troubleshooting**: one-liner only — "Check logs in `logs/`, verify your `.env` file, and see `docs/developer-guide.md`."
9. **Contributing**: one-liner only — "PRs welcome. Run `make format lint test` before submitting."
10. **Acknowledgments**: one line, no bullets.
11. **Requirements section**: 4 lines (Python 3.12+, SQLite3, libmagic, bot token).
12. **Commits/lint/test**: `make format lint` before committing, `make test` after any change.

title: Sandbox v1 architecture: three-axis split (Backend/Runtime/Manager Protocols)
content:
The sandbox system is designed with three orthogonal protocols:

1. **Backend protocol** (`Backend`) — containerization/execution backend. Only Docker in v0 (`BackendName.DOCKER`), but the protocol is designed upfront so Firecracker or other backends can be added later without changing callers.
2. **Runtime protocol** (`Runtime`) — language-specific execution environment. Only Python in v0 (`RuntimeName.PYTHON`), but TypeScript/Bash/Ruby can be added later via the same interface.
3. **Manager** (`SandboxManager`) — singleton that orchestrates Backend + Runtime. Owns the session lifecycle, FIFO queue, MetadataStore, and library pool.

Key conventions from this design: RuntimeName and BackendName are StrEnum types (from `lib/sandbox/enums.py`), used everywhere instead of raw strings. `RuntimeName.PYTHON = "python"`, `BackendName.DOCKER = "docker"`. Container and install image names are derived from these enums.

title: Sandbox v1: Libraries are runtime-scoped, admin-managed, RO-mounted
content:
Libraries in the sandbox system are NOT per-session or per-run. They are per-runtime (e.g., all Python sessions share the same library pool). The library pool lives at `${rootDir}/runtimes/<runtimeName>/libs/` on the host and is mounted RO into every session container.

Key design points:
- The install container is the only process that writes to the lib pool (protected by `fcntl.flock`)
- `runCode()` never installs packages — if `requiredPackages` are absent, it raises `MissingDependenciesError` without starting anything
- Admin API: `installRuntimeLibraries()`, `removeRuntimeLibraries()`, `listRuntimeLibraries()`
- After every install/remove, `pip freeze` output is captured as a snapshot in the metadata store for migration/audit purposes
- No package deny-list — admin responsibility to not install dangerous packages
- Bootstrap via `scripts/sandbox-bootstrap.py`, driven from `sandbox.bootstrap.starter_packages` TOML config key
- Alpine base image for both run and install containers. Only `build-base` is included from the heavy compile toolchain in the install image (Dockerfile.install: `python3 py3-pip py3-wheel py3-setuptools build-base git libmagic sqlite tzdata`). Packages like `gfortran`, `openblas-dev`, `openssl-dev`, `libffi-dev`, and `cargo` are NOT present — source builds requiring these will fail on musllinux. The run image stays minimal with no build toolchain.

title: Sandbox v1: stdout/stderr redirected to files, timeout wrapper, container naming
content:
Three concrete execution decisions in the sandbox v1 design:

1. **stdout/stderr → files** (not docker logs): Output is redirected to `stdout.log` and `stderr.log` via shell redirection inside the container. Portable across non-Docker backends.

2. **timeout wrapper on every run**: Commands wrap with `timeout -s TERM -k <graceSecs> <runTimeoutSecs> sh -c '...'`. Exit code 124 detection sets `timedOut=True` on RunResult. Belt-and-braces: Docker's own `asyncio.wait_for` with `watchdogTimeout` (timeoutSeconds + timeoutGraceSeconds + 1) still applies.

3. **Container naming**: NOT uniform. Three patterns used:
   - Run containers: `sandbox-<runId>` (uses run ID, not UUID)
   - Install containers: `sandbox-install-<uuid.uuid4().hex>` (full UUID hex string)
   - List containers: `sandbox-list-<uuid.uuid4().hex>`

4. **No tmpfs anywhere**: Only the bind-mounted workspace and RO lib mount are writable/readable. No tmpfs filesystem in containers.

title: Sandbox v1: MetadataStore Protocol with pluggable backends
Sandbox v1: Session/Run lifecycle and concurrency model
content:
Session and run lifecycle in the sandbox v1 design:

**Sessions**: Opaque string IDs, auto-created by `runCode()` with config defaults (default runtime, default TTL). Ephemeral containers but persistent workspace volume. `dropSession(force=False)` waits for in-flight run on FIFO queue then drops; `force=True` SIGKILLs running container, drains queue (SessionDropped on all waiters), then drops. `resetSession` was removed — identical to dropSession + createSession from caller's view.

**Runs**: Never auto-install packages — `requiredPackages` is a precondition check against the lib pool. If missing → `MissingDependenciesError`. SessionHash derived from full SHA-256 (64 hex chars) of sessionId.

**Concurrency model**: Per-session FIFO asyncio.Lock with bounded queue (overflow → `SandboxBusy`). Global concurrency semaphore on top. NetworkPolicy dataclass with just `enabled: bool` today, passed per-run (not stored in SessionInfo).

**Run retention**: Everything deleted as one unit (directory + contents). Workspace directory listing available via `listFiles()` method (returns list[FileInfo], supports recursive walk via rglob with per-file OSError guard). `getSessionUsage()` was planned but not implemented — no SessionUsage type exists. Prometheus metrics not implemented in current version.

title: Sandbox v1: Gromozeka integration split into separate design document
content:
The sandbox v1 design intentionally separates the core library from Gromozeka integration into two documents:

1. `docs/plans/python-sandboxing-v1.md` — the standalone sandbox library design (lib/sandbox/). No Gromozeka dependencies.
2. `docs/plans/python-sandboxing-v1-integration.md` — Gromozeka-specific glue: SandboxService singleton in `internal/services/sandbox/`, TOML config mapping `[sandbox.*]`, `RunPythonHandler` and `SandboxAdminHandler` (registered BEFORE LLMMessageHandler), `chatId+threadId` → `sessionId` mapping, bot_owners admin gating, and doc-sync checklist.

Clean layering: `lib/sandbox/` has no bot dependencies. `internal/services/sandbox/` adapts it to Gromozeka's conventions (singleton via getInstance(), service pattern).

title: Sandbox v1 design docs and implementation plan now in docs/plans/
content:
Three files produced from the June 10 2026 sandbox architecture session:

1. `docs/plans/python-sandboxing-v1.md` — Core sandbox library design (lib/sandbox/): Backend/Runtime/Manager protocols, Alpine base, runtime-scoped library pools, MetadataStore abstraction, full lifecycle, API surface, security model, GC, M1→M6 milestones.
2. `docs/plans/python-sandboxing-v1-integration.md` — Gromozeka glue: SandboxService singleton, TOML config, handlers, admin commands, doc-sync checklist, M5.1→M5.4 milestones.
3. `docs/plans/python-sandboxing-v1-implementation.md` — Teamlead-facing implementation plan with 24 work packages across 6 phases, dependency graph, specialist routing, risk register, verification gates per phase.

The implementation plan is structured for delegation: each WP has specialist assignment, dependencies, files to create/modify, acceptance criteria, test plan, and verify step. Cross-cutting rules block saves the teamlead from re-typing constraints. Reviewer passes inserted between phases.

title: Sandbox singleton: injectConfig() + getInstance() no-args pattern
content: The SandboxManager singleton uses a two-phase initialization: `SandboxManager.injectConfig(config)` stores the config in a class variable, then `SandboxManager.getInstance()` creates/returns the instance. `getInstance()` takes NO arguments. `__init__()` reads config from `cls._configInstance` directly, no config parameter. This avoids the anti-pattern of passing config to `getInstance()` and makes the interface cleaner.
