title: spam.py:520 markAsSpam is a SECOND correctness-critical messages_count reader; both gates now use refresh=True
content:
Extends/corrects memory c3cecb45-ba17-4fe0-bdac-a6f2653143cd (which documented only spam.py:275/checkSpam and recommended an invalidation hook in saveChatMessage as mitigation).

## Two correctness-critical messages_count readers found (not one)

Both live in `internal/bot/common/handlers/spam.py`:

1. **spam.py:~258 (checkSpam)** — feeds `userInfo["messages_count"]` (~line 275) into the `userMessages >= AUTO_SPAM_MAX_MESSAGES` gate (~277). A stale-LOW count lets a spammers sail past the "trusted user" threshold → under-checking spam. Mitigation: `refresh=True` on the feeding `cache.getChatUser`.

2. **spam.py:~526 (markAsSpam)** — feeds `userInfo["messages_count"]` (~line 520) into the `userInfo["messages_count"] > maxSpamMessages` gate, which REFUSES to mark the user as spam (protects established users from a false ban). A stale-LOW count makes an established user appear new → we ban a legit user. Same failure direction (stale-low → false ban of legit user). Mitigation: `refresh=True` on the feeding `cache.getChatUser`.

The second reader was NOT enumerated in the plan (§5/§14.A.4 only lists spam.py:275). It surfaced via the folded Phase 4 grep for `[\"messages_count\"]` / `.get(\"messages_count\")`.

## Decision resolution: refresh=True (option b), NOT the invalidation hook

c3cecb45 recommended adding an invalidation (or explicit `messages_count += 1`) hook inside `BaseBotHandler.saveChatMessage` (base.py:~1045). That recommendation was NOT adopted. The implemented decision (plan §15, decision A = option b) was: the spam gates read fresh via `refresh=True`, accepting the extra DB hit only on the two correctness-critical paths. The cache benefit is preserved for non-gated metadata/memory reads. `chat_search.py:840` (`u.get(\"messages_count\")`) reads from an aggregate `getChatUsers` query (hits DB directly, no cache) — correctly left out of scope.

## Takeaway for future readers
If you add a NEW single-row getChatUser read that feeds a `messages_count` comparison, check whether the comparison is correctness-critical (ban/refuse-to-ban gate). If yes, pass `refresh=True` to the feeding `cache.getChatUser` call. Document it inline (both spam.py sites have an explanatory comment).

title: Handler tests need no rewiring when routing through CacheService (injectDatabase flow-through pattern)
content:
Convention confirmed during the Phase 3 chat_users cache refactor (all single-row `db.chatUsers.*` calls in `internal/bot/common/handlers/` were moved to `handler.cache.*`, 244 handler tests, zero rewrites needed).

## Why no test rewiring was needed

The real-DB-backed handler tests (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_base.py`, `test_user_data.py`) construct the handler against the REAL `CacheService` singleton with `testDatabase` injected:

```python
CacheService._instance = None  # autouse reset per test
cache = CacheService.getInstance()
cache.injectDatabase(testDatabase)  # binds the cache to the test DB
handler = SomeHandler(database=testDatabase, cache=cache, ...)
```

Because the cache starts cold each test (singleton reset) and is wired to the same SQLite the test sets up and verifies against, every `cache.getChatUser`/`getUserMetadata`/`updateUserMetadata` transparently falls through to the DB on a miss and write-throughs on mutation. So:
- Direct `testDatabase.chatUsers.updateChatUser(...)` / `updateUserMetadata(...)` setup calls still work (they hit the same DB).
- Direct `testDatabase.chatUsers.getChatUser(...)` verification calls still see the data (the cache wrote it through).
- No need to re-stub at `handler.cache.*`.

## When you DO need to rewire
ONLY when a test patches `CacheService.getInstance` to a plain `Mock()` (e.g. `test_message_preprocessor.py`, `test_dev_commands.py`) AND the test actually exercises a refactored code path. In Phase 3 those Mock-cache tests did NOT exercise the join/leave/updateChatUser paths, so their `db.chatUsers.updateChatUser = AsyncMock(...)` stubs were unused defensive setup — left as-is. If they HAD exercised the path, `await handler.cache.updateChatUser(...)` on a plain Mock would raise (Mock is not awaitable) → fix by setting `handler.cache.updateChatUser = AsyncMock(...)`.

## Takeaway
Prefer the real-DB + injectDatabase pattern for handler tests that touch cache-backed data; it survives cache-layer refactors automatically. When a Mock-cache is necessary, make the specific method an AsyncMock at the assertion site.

title: Hot-path regression test pattern: AsyncMock(wraps=) class spy + stub updateChatInfo to bypass _bot
content:
Established pattern for end-to-end regression tests proving the write-through `chat_users` cache eliminates redundant DB reads on the message hot path (first applied in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_user_info_cache_regression.py`, 2026-07-05). This operates at the **handler-method level** — between raw cache unit tests (`tests/services/cache/test_user_info.py`) and the full `newMessageHandler` chain (too heavy: needs `_bot`, media processing, full `EnsuredMessage` + handler pipeline).

## GOTCHA: `saveChatMessage` calls `updateChatInfo` first, which needs `self._bot`
`BaseBotHandler.saveChatMessage` (internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py ~1004) calls `await self.updateChatInfo(message)` BEFORE the hot-path `await self.cache.updateChatUser(...)`. `updateChatInfo` reads `self._bot` and raises `ValueError` if it is None. To test the hot path in isolation, stub it: `cast(Any, handler).updateChatInfo = AsyncMock(return_value=None)`. Everything else in `saveChatMessage` runs real (the `cache.updateChatUser` write + `db.chatMessages.saveChatMessage` DB write).

## The spy pattern: `AsyncMock(wraps=originalMethod)` at CLASS level
`ChatUsersRepository` has `__slots__ = ()` (memory 76435069), so instance-level `patch.object` fails. Spy at the CLASS level instead, wrapping the original so the real DB still works AND the call is recorded:
```python
original = ChatUsersRepository.updateChatUser
with patch.object(ChatUsersRepository, "updateChatUser", AsyncMock(wraps=original)) as spy:
    ...drive the hot path...
    assert spy.call_count == 0  # skip-when-unchanged
```
Same for `ChatUsersRepository.getChatUser`.

## Full setup checklist (extends memory 814d7aa8's reset+inject pattern)
1. Autouse fixture resets `CacheService._instance` + `QueueService._instance` per test.
2. `cache = CacheService.getInstance()`; `await cache.injectDatabase(testDatabase)`; construct `MessagePreprocessorHandler` after injection (handler.cache === injected cache).
3. Pre-seed the `(chat, user)` row via `testDatabase.chatUsers.updateChatUser(...)`; warm the cache via `await handler.cache.getChatUser(chatId, userId)`.
4. Stub `handler.updateChatInfo` (see gotcha above).
5. Build a real `EnsuredMessage` with `messageType=MessageType.TEXT` (UNKNOWN causes early `return False`) and a sender whose username/fullName MATCH the seeded row.
6. Drive: `await handler.saveChatMessage(message, messageCategory=MessageCategory.USER)` then `await handler.getUserMemorySummary(chatId, userId, threadId)`.

## Headline assertions (warm cache + unchanged sender)
- `ChatUsersRepository.updateChatUser` call_count == 0 (skip-when-unchanged fires)
- `ChatUsersRepository.getChatUser` call_count == 0 (warm cache hit — `getUserMemorySummary` → `cache.getUserMetadata` → `cache.getChatUser`, all warm)

Counterpoints (prove the cache isn't swallowing everything): changed username → `updateChatUser` call_count >= 1; cold cache → `getChatUser` call_count >= 1.

title: Warm-cache "0 DB calls" regression tests are vacuous unless the spy wraps the real method
content:
When writing a regression test that asserts "0 DB reads/writes" on a warm write-through cache hit (e.g. the chat_users cache), the spy MUST use `AsyncMock(wraps=realBoundMethod)` so the REAL DB still runs — NOT a plain `AsyncMock(return_value=cannedRow)`.

Failure mode if ignored: a plain `AsyncMock(return_value=...)` REPLACES the repo method entirely. The cache "hits" the mock's canned row instead of genuinely warming itself from a real DB read on the first miss. The "0 calls" assertion then passes TRIVIALLY (the mock never falls through to a real read), so the test proves NOTHING about the cache's skip logic. This is a silent correctness bug in the test itself — it passes but establishes no real invariant.

The correct shape (verified on tests/bot/common/handlers/test_user_info_cache_regression.py, headline test `test_warmCache_unchangedSender_zeroChatUsersDbReadsAndWrites`):

1. Seed a real DB row DIRECTLY via the repo (bypassing the cache) → cache stays cold.
2. Call `cache.getChatUser(...)` once → genuine miss → real DB read → populates `userInfo` → cache now genuinely WARM.
3. Install class-level spies: capture `original = repo.method` BEFORE patching, then `with patch.object(RepoClass, "method", new=AsyncMock(wraps=original))`. The `wraps=` target is the real bound method, so on any fall-through the real DB runs AND the call is recorded.
4. Drive the hot path (e.g. `handler.saveChatMessage`). Because the cache is genuinely warm and the sender is unchanged, `cache.updateChatUser` skips → spy.call_count == 0 for BOTH get and update. This is a meaningful proof, not vacuous.

The counterpoint tests (changed username → `updateChatUser.call_count >= 1`; cold cache → `getChatUser.call_count >= 1`) are only meaningful under the same `wraps=` discipline — a plain mock would record calls against itself and also be vacuous.

This extends memory 76435069 (which says to use `wraps=` but doesn't explain the vacuous-test trap). The `__slots__ = ()` requirement for class-level patching and the "capture bound method before patch" timing rule are all in 76435069 — do not re-derive them.

Prefer deterministic `== N` over `>= 1` assertions where the call count is genuinely fixed (warm-skip path = exactly 0; one cold read = exactly 1; one changed-username write = exactly 1), so the test also catches UNEXPECTED extra calls, not just absence/presence.

title: Chat-member handler tests' exact-args assertions don't catch setUserMetadata merge regressions (getUserMetadata mocked to {})
content:
The two Phase 5 tests in `TestChatMemberHandlers` (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_message_preprocessor.py`):
- `test_newChatMemberHandler_routesUpdateChatUserThroughCache` (~L590)
- `test_leftChatMemberHandler_routesUpdateChatUserThroughCache` (~L617)

were tightened to use `cache.updateUserMetadata.assert_awaited_once_with(chatId=…, userId=…, metadata={"leftChat": …})`. Their inline comments claim to pin the shallow-merged dict produced by `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` at `base.py:1083-1106` (`existing = cache.getUserMetadata(...)`; `metadata = {**existing, **metadata}`).

**These assertions do NOT actually detect a dropped-merge regression.** The test fixture `_wireCacheForChatMember` mocks `cache.getUserMetadata` to return `{}`, so `{**{}, **{"leftChat": …}}` is identical to `{"leftChat": …}`. If someone deletes the merge line entirely, `updateUserMetadata` receives the same dict and the assertion still passes. This gap is especially relevant given the existing BLOCKER gotcha (memory 3c6a5fbc): the shallow-merge in `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` can destroy sibling nested keys like `memoryRefinement` — a regression these tests would silently miss.

**What the assertions DO catch:** wrong chatId/userId routing (e.g. swapped join/leave args), wrong metadata key/value (e.g. flipped leftChat), or a handler that bypasses setUserMetadata and calls updateUserMetadata with a different dict. This is a strict improvement over bare `assert_awaited_once()`.

**To genuinely detect merge regressions**, the mock must return a non-empty baseline so a dropped merge clobbers it:
```python
cache.getUserMetadata = AsyncMock(return_value={"memoryRefinement": {"0": {"summary": "x"}}})
```
then assert the merged dict retains the sibling key, e.g. on join:
```python
cache.updateUserMetadata.assert_awaited_once_with(
    chatId=100, userId=7, metadata={"memoryRefinement": {"0": {"summary": "x"}}, "leftChat": False}
)
```
This was flagged to the user but NOT implemented (beyond the stated polish scope). The test files were the only thing changed in that session.

title: Testing discipline: non-empty baseline required to assert a shallow-merge happened
content:
When a test asserts the *output* of a `{**existing, **new}` shallow merge via a mock (e.g. `updateUserMetadata.assert_awaited_once_with(..., metadata=<merged dict>)`), the mock supplying `existing` MUST return a **non-empty** dict containing a sentinel sibling key. If it returns `{}`, then `{**{}, **new}` is identical to `new` — a regression that deletes the merge line entirely produces the same recorded dict and the assertion passes tautologically.

Correct shape:
```python
cache.getUserMetadata = AsyncMock(return_value={"memoryRefinement": {"0": {"summary": "pre-existing"}}})
# then assert the merged dict RETAINS the sibling key:
cache.updateUserMetadata.assert_awaited_once_with(
    chatId=..., userId=...,
    metadata={"memoryRefinement": {"0": {"summary": "pre-existing"}}, "leftChat": ...},
)
```

This bit the project once: chat-member handler tests in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_message_preprocessor.py` had inline comments claiming to detect a dropped-merge regression in `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` (`base.py:1105`, `metadata = {**existing, **metadata}`), while the `{}` baseline made the claim false. The fix (non-empty baseline + sibling key in the expected dict) was applied 2026-07-05; the production merge was confirmed correct (2895 tests pass).

Relevance: the shallow-merge in `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` is itself a known-BLOCKER footgun (memory 3c6a5fbc) — it can destroy sibling nested keys like `memoryRefinement`. Tests that guard it must therefore actually be able to detect its absence. Apply this pattern to any future test that pins the result of a dict merge.

title: chat_users write-through cache COMPLETE — ADR-015; ChatUsersRepository __slots__ test gotcha
content:
The write-through `chat_users` cache in `CacheService` is FULLY IMPLEMENTED (2026-07-05, branch `memory-refinement`, 2895 tests green). All phases done — cache layer + all call-site refactoring. Authoritative documentation: **ADR-015** in `docs/llm/architecture.md`. Plan: `docs/plans/user-info-cache-plan-v1.md` (status: IMPLEMENTED).

Implementation facts (verify against ADR-015/code, not this memory):

The namespace now backs BOTH the `user_data` table (`data` field, via getChatUserData/setChatUserData) AND the `chat_users` row (`userInfo` field). Keyed `f"{chatId}:{userId}"`.
- 5 new `CacheService` methods (service.py, grouped under `# ## ChatUser UserInfo`): `getChatUser(chatId,userId,*,refresh=False)`, `updateChatUser(chatId,userId,username,fullName)`, `getUserMetadata(chatId,userId)`, `updateUserMetadata(chatId,userId,metadata)`, `invalidateChatUser(chatId,userId)` (sync, pops only `userInfo`, preserves `data`).
- All single-row `(chatId,userId)` reads/writes in the handler layer route through `self.cache.*`, NOT `self.db.chatUsers.*`. Files: base.py, spam.py, message_preprocessor.py, user_data.py. Aggregate/by-username queries untouched.
- `messages_count` is stale in cache (incremented by raw SQL at `chat_messages.py:154`, bypasses cache). `spam.py` checkSpam/markAsSpam use `refresh=True`.
- `updateUserMetadata` does NO merge — callers must read-full, mutate-nested, write-full (nested-write invariant).

TEST WRITING GOTCHA (still valid, from the implementation phase): `ChatUsersRepository` uses `__slots__ = ()`, so `patch.object(repoInstance, method)` FAILS with AttributeError. Patch at the CLASS level: `patch.object(ChatUsersRepository, "getChatUser", new=AsyncMock(wraps=original))`, capturing the bound method before patching.

title: Convention: adding a cache/abstraction layer makes existing direct-repo doc guidance a bypass footgun — grep all docs
content:
When implementing a write-through cache (or any new abstraction layer) over a DB repository, ALL pre-existing documentation that recommends calling the repository directly becomes a latent footgun: callers following the old guidance silently bypass the cache and cause cache-DB divergence (the exact desync the cache was meant to prevent).

Observed during the chat_users cache docs task (2026-07-05): four independent docs — `docs/database-schema.md`, `docs/database-schema-llm.md`, `docs/llm/tasks.md` §3, and `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` — all consistently recommended `self.db.chatUsers.updateUserMetadata(...)` directly. After the write-through cache landed, that guidance became actively dangerous (bypasses `CacheService.updateUserMetadata`). All four were corrected to route through `self.cache.*`.

LESSON for future cache/abstraction-layer features: after changing the canonical access path, grep ALL of `docs/` for references to the old direct-repo path (`db.<repo>.<method>`, `chatUsers.`, etc.) and update them — do not limit the sweep to the files the task explicitly scopes. The task's 7-item doc list did NOT name these stale references; they were found by proactive search. Apply this whenever the canonical call path for any repository moves behind a service.

title: updateUserMetadata returns True on 0-row UPDATE (absent row) — cache write-through guard can't detect silent no-op
content:
`ChatUsersRepository.updateUserMetadata(chatId, userId, metadata: str) -> bool` (internal/database/repositories/chat_users.py:126) executes a raw `UPDATE chat_users SET ... WHERE chat_id=:chatId AND user_id=:userId` and returns `True` as long as `execute()` doesn't raise — regardless of how many rows matched. If the `chat_users` row does NOT exist, the UPDATE is a SQL no-op but the method returns `True`.

This is a pre-existing repo quirk, but it has a NEW consequence now that the write-through cache wraps it: `CacheService.updateUserMetadata` does `ok = await db.chatUsers.updateUserMetadata(...); if not ok: return` before touching the cache. Since `ok` is `True` even on a 0-row UPDATE, the guard NEVER fires for an absent row. The metadata write is silently lost, and if the row IS cached (None sentinel), the cache is not mutated (correct by accident — the `if cached is not None` re-read branch handles it). But the write is gone with no error.

Mitigation in practice: `updateChatUser` (the full-row upsert) is always called BEFORE `updateUserMetadata` on the message hot path (saveChatMessage calls `cache.updateChatUser` first, which creates the row). So in the normal flow the row exists by the time metadata is written. The risk is only in code paths that write metadata WITHOUT a prior `updateChatUser` upsert for that (chatId, userId) — those writes silently vanish if the row was never created.

Discovered during Gate 2 code review of the chat_users write-through cache (2026-07-05, branch memory-refinement). Review verdict: pre-existing behavior, not a regression, but worth knowing when adding new metadata-writing code paths.

title: Username @-sign normalization inconsistency defeats cache skip-when-unchanged optimization
content:
`CacheService.updateChatUser` skip-when-unchanged guard compares `cached["username"] == username and cached["full_name"] == fullName`. The `ChatUsersRepository.updateChatUser` docstring says username "should be with @ sign", but there is no centralized normalization — callers pass whatever the platform provides, and the DB stores whatever was passed on the last upsert.

If some callers pass `"alice"` and others pass `"@alice"` for the same user, the equality check will fail on every message, defeating the skip optimization and forcing an unnecessary DB upsert per message (the exact redundancy the cache was built to eliminate). This is a pre-existing inconsistency (not introduced by the cache), but the cache makes it more impactful because it gates the skip optimization.

Fix direction: normalize username formatting (strip/ensure leading `@`) at a single boundary — ideally in `MessageSender` construction or in `updateChatUser` itself — before the comparison. Not yet fixed as of 2026-07-05.

Discovered during Gate 2 code review of the chat_users write-through cache. Classified as NIT (pre-existing, performance-only, no correctness impact).

title: Conditional-refresh microopt: refresh predicate depends on gate comparison operator (>= vs >)
content:
Extends memories fe1cefef and c090f6db (which documented the two unconditional `refresh=True` sites in spam.py for the stale-LOW messages_count problem).

## The subtle trap when converting unconditional refresh=True to a conditional microopt

A proposed simplification replaced the two unconditional `cache.getChatUser(refresh=True)` calls in `spam.py` with a helper `_getUserInfoFreshIfMessagesLessThan(chatId, userId, threshold)` that reads the cached value first and only refreshes when `cached["messages_count"] < threshold`. The premise is sound: `messages_count` is monotonically non-decreasing (bumped by raw SQL UPDATE in saveChatMessage, bypassing the cache), so a cached at-or-above-threshold value is still at-or-above-threshold in the DB.

## But the two gates have DIFFERENT comparison operators, requiring DIFFERENT refresh predicates

- **checkSpam gate (spam.py:~282)**: `userMessages >= maxCheckMessages` ("treat as trusted ham"). A `>=` gate is SAFE with a `<` refresh predicate: if cached == threshold, no refresh, check `cached >= threshold` → True → trusted; fresh value is also >= threshold → also trusted. ✓ Correct.

- **markAsSpam gate (spam.py:~545)**: `userInfo["messages_count"] > maxSpamMessages` ("protect established user from ban"). A strict `>` gate is UNSAFE with a `<` refresh predicate: if cached == threshold, no refresh (cached is not < threshold), check `cached > threshold` → False → ban proceeds. But the true fresh count (post-saveChatMessage increment) may be `threshold + N` for an established user → **FALSE BAN of a legit user.** This re-opens the exact bug ADR-015 was designed to close. ✗ BUG.

## The rule

When a `messages_count` comparison gate is converted from unconditional `refresh=True` to a conditional refresh, the refresh predicate MUST match the gate operator:
- Gate uses `>=` → refresh when `cached < threshold` (the boundary cached==threshold needs no refresh).
- Gate uses strict `>` → refresh when `cached <= threshold` (the boundary cached==threshold DOES need refresh, because fresh may now be threshold+1).

Parameterise the helper (e.g. `inclusiveThreshold: bool` or `operator: Literal["<", "<="]`) or split into two helpers. Do NOT use a single `<` predicate for both gates. Also: cached values drift LOW (the raw UPDATE bypasses the cache), never high — stale-low is the only risk direction, but the boundary case still bites.

## Correction to prior guidance
Memory fe1cefef says "if you add a NEW correctness-critical messages_count reader, it must use refresh=True". That's true but incomplete: if you replace an EXISTING unconditional refresh=True with a conditional microopt, re-derive the refresh predicate from the gate's comparison operator, don't blindly reuse `<`.

title: None-sentinel for absent chat_users row is load-bearing — removing it causes per-message DB re-query storms
content:
Complements memory afcf193e (which documents the None-sentinel design for `HCChatUserCacheDict.userInfo`).

## The invariant that must not be dropped

The chat_users cache design relies on memoizing "row genuinely absent in DB" to avoid re-querying on every read. The original representation:
- key absent (`"userInfo" not in entry`) = "not yet loaded"
- `userInfo: None` = "loaded, row is absent" (the None sentinel)

A proposed simplification dropped `Optional[]` from the field type (`NotRequired[Optional[ChatUserDict]]` → `NotRequired[ChatUserDict]`) and, to match, changed `getChatUser` to return None immediately on a DB miss WITHOUT storing the sentinel. This broke the invariant.

## Why dropping it is a regression

Once the sentinel is gone and absent rows are not cached:
- `getChatUser` re-queries the DB on EVERY call for any `(chatId, userId)` whose row genuinely doesn't exist yet. For a new sender, the chat_users row is created by `updateChatUser` (message_preprocessor) — but until then, every inbound message from that user re-queries.
- The cold path in `updateChatUser` that re-read the row to warm the cache was also removed as part of the simplification (because without None it couldn't distinguish "absent, just upserted" from "absent, never tried"). This compounds the issue.
- The synthetic-dict fallback in `spam.py:~278-288` is built on the very case where getChatUser returns None (new users) — exactly the users most likely to be genuinely-absent and thus repeatedly re-queried.

## If you simplify the type away, use a different absent-marker

To keep memoization with a non-Optional field type, use a private sentinel object instead of None:
```python
_ABSENT_SENTINEL = object()
# in getChatUser, on DB miss:
userCache["userInfo"] = _ABSENT_SENTINEL  # memoize absence
# in all readers, check `is _ABSENT_SENTINEL` before use
```
The TypedDict can stay `NotRequired[ChatUserDict]` at the type-checker level if the sentinel is a private CacheService implementation detail. Or revert to `Optional[ChatUserDict]` for type honesty. Either way: the absent-row case MUST be memoized. Do NOT just return None and leave the cache cold.

## ADR-015 contract
`docs/llm/architecture.md` ADR-015 (~line 517) explicitly states the "absent row is not re-queried every call" property as part of the contract. Any change that removes it must either restore memoization or update the ADR and explicitly accept the per-message re-query cost.

title: chat_users cache POST-REVIEW simplified contract (supersedes Optional+None-sentinel)
content:
The write-through `chat_users` cache was SIMPLIFIED post-review (branch `memory-refinement`, aligned 2026-07-05, 2899 tests green). This memory is the CURRENT authoritative contract. It SUPERSEDES the Optional/None-sentinel + unconditional-`refresh=True` descriptions in memories fa83405c, fe1cefef, and c090f6db — those describe the PRE-simplification state and are now stale on these points. Canonical docs: **ADR-015** in `docs/llm/architecture.md` + `## §16 Post-review simplification` addendum in `docs/plans/user-info-cache-plan-v1.md`.

## The four key changes vs. the earlier contract

1. **`userInfo` is non-Optional now.** `HCChatUserCacheDict.userInfo: NotRequired[ChatUserDict]` (was `NotRequired[Optional[ChatUserDict]]`). Presence-of-key is the "loaded" signal; there is NO None-sentinel. Keyed `f"{chatId}:{userId}"` in `CacheNamespace.CHAT_USERS`.

2. **`getChatUser` does NOT cache absent rows.** On hit (not refresh) → return `cached.copy()`. On miss/refresh → `db.chatUsers.getChatUser(...)`; row found → store under `userInfo` + return `.copy()`; **row absent → return None WITHOUT setting `userInfo`** (intentional — an absent user indicates something went wrong; not worth memoizing). A second call therefore re-queries the DB. NOTE: on `refresh=True` with a stale `userInfo` already cached, an absent DB row returns None but leaves the stale `userInfo` in place (quirk, not documented as cleared).

3. **`updateChatUser` cold path leaves the cache cold.** Warm cached row with matching username AND full_name → skip DB entirely. Else `ok = await db.chatUsers.updateChatUser(...)`; `if not ok: return`; **warm → mutate cached row in place** (username/full_name/updated_at via `dbUtils.getCurrentTimestamp()`); **cold → leave cache cold** (NO re-read to warm — intentional; the row may never be read again, and the next `getChatUser` lazy-loads if needed).

4. **`updateUserMetadata`/`getUserMetadata`/`invalidateChatUser` unchanged** from the prior contract: write-through with `if not ok: return`; warm mutate in place; cold leave cold; NO merge (callers must read-full/mutate-nested/write-full); `invalidateChatUser` (sync) pops ONLY `userInfo`, preserves `data`.

## Tests for this contract
- `tests/services/cache/test_user_info.py` was rewritten: `test_getChatUser_absentRowReturnsNoneAndDoesNotCache` (absent→None, cache cold, re-query), `test_updateChatUser_coldUpsertsAndLeavesCacheCold` (DB upsert once, `getChatUser` NOT called).
- The old test names (`...AndCachesSentinel`, `...ThenWarmsViaReRead`) no longer exist — if you see them referenced, they're stale.

title: spam messages_count microopt: conditional refresh + markAsSpam +1 boundary trick
content:
The `messages_count` staleness mitigation in `internal/bot/common/handlers/spam.py` was changed from UNCONDITIONAL `refresh=True` (as documented in memories c090f6db / fe1cefef) to a CONDITIONAL-refresh microoptimization. This SUPERSEDES those memories' "use `refresh=True` at both spam gates" guidance. Line numbers shifted: the helper now lives ~spam.py:202, `checkSpam` call ~273, `markAsSpam` call ~543.

## The helper
`_getUserInfoFreshIfMessagesLessThan(self, chatId, userId, messagesCountThreshold)` (NOTE: the old param `messagesCountTreshold` was a typo — missing `h` — and was renamed to `messagesCountThreshold` for correct spelling + AGENTS.md camelCase):
- Reads cached userInfo via `cache.getChatUser(chatId, userId)` (no refresh).
- If `not userInfo` (None / cold) → return it (None), no refresh.
- If `userInfo["messages_count"] < messagesCountThreshold` → re-fetch via `cache.getChatUser(chatId, userId, refresh=True)`; else return the cached value.
- **Rationale:** `messages_count` is monotonically non-decreasing, so a cached at-or-above-threshold value remains valid for the comparison; refresh only fires when the cached value is below threshold and might have grown.

## The two call sites and their gates (CRITICAL boundary detail)
- **`checkSpam`** uses a `>=` gate (`userMessages >= maxCheckMessages`). Passes `messagesCountThreshold=maxCheckMessages`. So: cached `==` threshold → no refresh (correct, since `>=` holds whether or not the true count drifted up).
- **`markAsSpam`** uses a STRICT `>` gate (`userInfo["messages_count"] > maxSpamMessages`, which REFUSES to ban established users). Passes `messagesCountThreshold=maxSpamMessages+1` (EXACT source form: `messagesCountThreshold=maxSpamMessages+1`, no spaces). The `+1` is load-bearing: it makes the helper's strict-`<` fire when `cached == maxSpamMessages`, i.e. exactly the boundary case where a stale-low count would wrongly classify an established user as new → false ban. Without the `+1`, `cached == maxSpamMessages` would skip refresh and the stale-low value would pass the `>` check incorrectly.

## When adding a NEW `messages_count` comparison reader
Use the helper (or `refresh=True` only if the conditional form can't apply). Check whether the gate is `>=`/`>` — a strict-`>` gate MUST pass `threshold+1` to the helper, else the boundary false-ban window reopens. The helper docstring records this caveat. Tests: `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_spam_microopt.py` (4 cases incl. the boundary).

title: Test pattern: unit-test single SpamHandler method via __new__ + mock cache
content:
To unit-test a single pure-logic helper on `SpamHandler` (e.g. `_getUserInfoFreshIfMessagesLessThan`) without standing up the heavy `__init__` (which needs ConfigManager, Database, BotProvider, and a Bayes filter), use `SpamHandler.__new__(SpamHandler)` to bypass `__init__` entirely, then attach only the attributes the helper touches:

```python
handler = SpamHandler.__new__(SpamHandler)
getChatUser = AsyncMock(return_value=row)
cache = AsyncMock()
cache.getChatUser = getChatUser
handler.cache = cache
```

`SpamHandler` (like other handlers) has no `__slots__`, so instance attributes can be set freely. This is the established pattern in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_spam_microopt.py` and mirrors the `HandlersManager.__new__` approach in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_manager.py`.

PYRIGHT GOTCHA: do NOT assert on `handler.cache.getChatUser.call_count` directly via the real-typed `handler.cache` — pyright sees `cache` as the concrete `CacheService` and rejects `.call_count` on a bound method. Instead, have the test helper return a `(handler, getChatUserMock)` tuple and assert on the local `AsyncMock` reference (avoids needing `cast(AsyncMock, ...)` chains or `# type: ignore`).

title: AsyncMock return_value sameness makes refresh-path value assertions vacuous — use side_effect
content:
When testing a conditional-refresh / read-through helper (e.g. a method that first reads a cache then optionally re-fetches with `refresh=True`), do NOT mock the underlying call with `AsyncMock(return_value=singleObject)`. That returns the SAME object on every call, so an assertion on the returned value (e.g. `row["messages_count"] == 3`) is VACUOUS: it passes whether or not the helper actually performed and assigned the refresh result. A helper that calls refresh but forgets to reassign the result (`if x < threshold: await ...; # forgot userInfo = await ...`) would still pass the test.

This surfaced in code review of `SpamHandler._getUserInfoFreshIfMessagesLessThan` tests (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_spam_microopt.py`). The tests there correctly differentiate the refresh path via `getSpy.call_count == 2` and a `_refreshWasCalled(getSpy)` helper that inspects `call_args_list` for `refresh=True` kwargs — so they are NOT vacuous as-is. But the review recommended strengthening two of them (cached-below-threshold + boundary sub-case 2) to be fully behavioural.

The fix: give the spy a `side_effect` (callable or list) that returns a DISTINCT object on the refresh call (e.g. first call → `{messages_count: 3}`, second → `{messages_count: 12}`) and assert the helper returns the REFRESHED value. This converts a call-count test into a behavioural one.

Companion convention (confirmed good practice, used here): mock the DEPENDENCY (the cache), not the helper under test — so the real helper logic is exercised. Only the cache is an `AsyncMock`. Build the handler via `SpamHandler.__new__(SpamHandler)` and assign `handler.cache = mock` to bypass `__init__`.

Related existing memories: 8ff9b792 (createAsyncMock helper uses `sideEffect` camelCase kwarg, not `side_effect`).

title: Memory-refinement: >128-burst silently loses messages (accounting + cursor bugs)
content:
Identified in a fresh code review (2026-07-05, branch `memory-refinement`, commit range master..HEAD). NOT YET FIXED. Both issues share one trigger scenario: a single user sends >128 messages (`_memoryMaxMessagesPerRun`) between refinement ticks (busy chat, or bot was down). Located in `internal/bot/common/handlers/user_data.py`.

## Bug 1 — accounting subtracts preCount, not messages-actually-processed
In `_dtCronJob` (the cron scan + dispatch loop), the `finally` block decrements `self._accounting[key]` by `preCount` (the raw `newMessagesCount` snapshot at scan time) REGARDLESS of how many messages `_runRefinement` actually fed to the LLM. The docstring claims "decremented by the number of messages attempted (credit-consumed)" but `preCount` is the lifetime counter, not the attempted count. `_runRefinement` caps the fetch at 128.

Concrete failure (200-message burst):
- accounting[key]=200, count threshold (5) fires.
- `_runRefinement` fetches newest 128, processes them, advances cursor.
- finally subtracts 200 → accounting[key]=0, key dropped.
- The 72 older messages are now before the cursor (see Bug 2).

## Bug 2 — cursor advances to newest-of-batch, making overflow permanently unreachable
`_runRefinement` sets `lastProcessedMessageDate` to `messages[0]["date"]` — the NEWEST of the fetched 128 (the fetch is newest-first). After a partial batch, the cursor jumps past ALL messages including the 72 unprocessed-older ones. `getChatMessagesSince(sinceDateTime=cursor)` only goes forward, so those 72 are never fetched again.

Even if Bug 1 were fixed (preserve leftover credit), the cursor jump means the next tick fetches only genuinely-new messages — the 72 remain lost.

## Reviewer's suggested fixes
- Bug 1: have `_runRefinement` RETURN the count of messages processed (or `None` on early-bail), and decrement accounting by THAT, not by preCount:
  ```python
  consumed = processed if processed is not None else preCount
  newVal = max(0, self._accounting.get(key, 0) - consumed)
  ```
- Bug 2: when `len(messages) >= _memoryMaxMessagesPerRun` (cap hit), advance cursor only to `messages[-1]["date"]` (oldest of batch) instead of `messages[0]`, so the next run pages forward through the remainder. Trades "newest-first priority" for "no data loss."

## Also noted (lower severity, same finally block)
On `_runRefinement` EXCEPTION, accounting is STILL decremented by preCount. A persistent LLM outage zeroes every active user's credit each tick; recovery only via 5-more-messages or the 6h time threshold. Acceptable as accidental backoff but worth knowing.

Self-healing note: if persistence of the cursor is lost to the metadata race (separate memory), next refinement re-reads the OLD cursor and reprocesses — so the bugs are partially self-masking. But the accounting wipe (Bug 1) means reprocessing only fires after credit re-accumulates.

title: Metadata read-modify-write race: _persistMemoryEntry vs setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)
content:
Identified in a code review (2026-07-05, branch `memory-refinement`). NOT YET FIXED. This is a concurrency gotcha that extends the documented "nested-write invariant" (memory fa83405c: `updateUserMetadata` does NO merge — every caller must read-full/mutate-nested/write-full). The invariant is followed, but TWO such read-modify-write writers can race each other because there is NO cross-writer lock.

## The race
- Writer A: `UserDataHandler._persistMemoryEntry` (in `internal/bot/common/handlers/user_data.py`, ~line 555-596) — called from `_runRefinement` under `_refineLock`. Reads metadata via `cache.getUserMetadata`, mutates only `metadata.memoryRefinement[str(threadId)]`, writes back via `cache.updateUserMetadata`.
- Writer B: `BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` (in `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py`, ~line 1083-1106) — called from message handlers (e.g. spam marking sets `isSpammer`/`autoDelete`/`leftChat`). Reads via `cache.getUserMetadata`, shallow-merges the new top-level keys, writes back via `cache.updateUserMetadata`.

`_refineLock` serializes refinement runs against EACH OTHER, but does NOT cover `setUserMetadata` callers in other handlers. Both reads can resolve before either write; the second write wins and silently overwrites the first.

## Concrete interleaving (single event loop, both writers have `await` between read and write):
1. Writer A reads `{memoryRefinement: {…}, isSpammer: false}`.
2. Writer B reads the same dict.
3. Writer A writes `{memoryRefinement: {new}, isSpammer: false}`.
4. Writer B writes `{memoryRefinement: {old}, isSpammer: true}` → A's memoryRefinement update is LOST.
(Ordering can flip, in which case a spammer flag gets dropped instead.)

This is partially self-healing for the refinement side: next refinement re-reads the old cursor and reprocesses. But it can silently drop a `isSpammer` flag in the opposite direction — NOT self-healing.

## Reviewer's suggested fix
The cache layer is the right place since it owns the row cache. Extend the existing `cache._chatUsersLock` (or add a dedicated metadata lock) and have BOTH `cache.updateUserMetadata` AND any merge-then-write caller take it across the FULL read-modify-write (read await → mutate → write await). Without this, the read and write awaits are separable yield points and the race window is open.

At minimum, document this as a known limitation in `docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md` so it's a conscious tradeoff, not a silent assumption. Also worth grepping the full tree for any `db.chatUsers.updateUserMetadata`/`updateChatUser` calls that bypass the cache (the review only audited the diff).

title: chat_users.metadata audit COMPLETE: CacheService.updateUserMetadata is the SOLE write path, no bypasses; full callsite map
content:
Closes the open question in memory e2eaf01a ("worth grepping the full tree for any db.chatUsers.updateUserMetadata/updateChatUser calls that bypass the cache"). The exhaustive grep (internal/, lib/, tests/) was performed on 2026-07-05. Result: **CacheService.updateUserMetadata is the SOLE write path for chat_users.metadata in production code. There are zero bypasses.**

## The funnel (single chokepoint)
The repository method `ChatUsersRepository.updateUserMetadata` (internal/database/repositories/chat_users.py, the raw `UPDATE chat_users SET metadata = ...`) has exactly **ONE production caller**: `CacheService.updateUserMetadata` (internal/services/cache/service.py:~1132). No handler, service, or lib code calls the repo method directly. No metadata writers exist in lib/ at all.

## The two `cache.updateUserMetadata` production callsites (both read-modify-write)
1. `BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata(chatId, userId, metadata, isUpdate=True)` (internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:~1083-1106) — reads via `cache.getUserMetadata`, shallow top-level merge `{**existing, **metadata}`, writes via `cache.updateUserMetadata`. This is the funnel for all 6 handler callsites below.
2. `UserDataHandler._persistMemoryEntry` (internal/bot/common/handlers/user_data.py:~588-596) — reads full metadata, mutates ONLY the nested `memoryRefinement[str(threadId)]` entry, writes full dict back. Deliberately bypasses `setUserMetadata` (documented CRITICAL in its docstring).

## The six `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` callsites (ALL read-modify-write)
| File:~line | Enclosing handler method | Metadata keys written |
|---|---|
| spam.py ~630 | `SpamHandler.markAsSpam` | `{isSpammer:True, notSpammer:False}` |
| spam.py ~1060 | `SpamHandler.callbackHandler` (ham-report button) | `{isSpammer:False, notSpammer:True}` |
| spam.py ~1701 | `SpamHandler.unban_command` | `{isSpammer:False, notSpammer:True, dropMessages:False}` |
| spam.py ~1784 | `SpamHandler.mark_for_delete_command` | `{dropMessages: isMark}` |
| message_preprocessor.py ~175 | `MessagePreprocessorHandler.newChatMemberHandler` | `{leftChat:False}` |
| message_preprocessor.py ~223 | `MessagePreprocessorHandler.leftChatMemberHandler` | `{leftChat:True}` |

## Raw-SQL `UPDATE chat_users` — only 2, only 1 touches metadata
- `chat_users.py` `updateUserMetadata` — writes `metadata` (the repo method above).
- `chat_messages.py:~154` — writes ONLY `messages_count` + `updated_at` (the documented messages_count cache-bypass, ADR-015). Does NOT write `metadata`, so it is IRRELEVANT to the metadata RMW race.

## `updateChatUser` does NOT touch metadata
`CacheService.updateChatUser` (service.py:~1050-1084) upserts only `username`/`full_name`/`updated_at`; the repo upsert's `updateExpressions` omit `metadata`, so metadata is preserved. NOT a metadata writer.

## Implication for the lock fix
A lock placed inside `CacheService` (covering getUserMetadata read + updateUserMetadata write across the full RMW) would cover EVERY metadata writer, because there are no bypasses. The race is purely between cache-layer callers: `_persistMemoryEntry` (under `_refineLock`) vs. the six `setUserMetadata` callers (NOT under `_refineLock`). (Line numbers are approximate as of 2026-07-05; re-verify with grep before editing.)

title: Correction: no _chatUsersLock exists in CacheService — e2eaf01a's "extend existing lock" advice is wrong
content:
Corrects memory e2eaf01a, which suggested fixing the metadata RMW race by "extending the existing `cache._chatUsersLock`". **There is no `_chatUsersLock`.** An exhaustive grep of internal/services/cache/service.py (2026-07-05) found only two locks, neither related to chat_users/metadata:

- `self.lock = RLock()` at service.py:~108 — instance-level general lock.
- `_lock: RLock = RLock()` at service.py:~230 — class-level lock, used ONLY for the singleton `getInstance()` guard.

`getChatUser`, `updateChatUser`, `getUserMetadata`, and `updateUserMetadata` perform NO locking around their read-modify-write windows. The cache mutation is entirely unsynchronized.

**Action for the implementer:** Do not look for an existing lock to extend. You must ADD a new dedicated metadata/chat_users lock from scratch (e.g. an `asyncio.Lock` keyed or instance-scoped inside `CacheService`) and have BOTH `cache.updateUserMetadata` AND any merge-then-write caller (`setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)`, `_persistMemoryEntry`) take it across the FULL read-modify-write (read await → mutate → write await). Note the existing locks use `threading.RLock` (sync) — a metadata RMW lock must be `asyncio.Lock` because the read and write are `await` points on a single event loop (a threading lock would not serialize across `await` yields).

title: chatUserMetadataLock implemented in CacheService — resolves metadata RMW race (09c498a1 fixed)
content:
Resolves memory `09c498a1` (was status "identified-unfixed") and supersedes the "add a new lock from scratch" action it recommended — that action has now been carried out (2026-07-05).

## What was implemented
`internal/services/cache/service.py` now has `self._chatUsersMetadataLock = asyncio.Lock()` (initialized inside the singleton `if not hasattr(self, "initialized"):` guard in `CacheService.__init__`, alongside `self.dirtyKeys`) and an async context manager:

```python
@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def chatUserMetadataLock(self):
    async with self._chatUsersMetadataLock:
        yield
```

Both read-modify-write callers of `chat_users.metadata` now hold it across the FULL RMW:
1. `BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py` — wraps `getUserMetadata` → merge → `updateUserMetadata`. The `isUpdate=False` direct-replace path stays OUTSIDE the lock (no read, no race).
2. `UserDataHandler._persistMemoryEntry` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/user_data.py` — wraps `getUserMetadata` → nested mutate → `updateUserMetadata`.

Plain reads (`getUserMetadata`) and full-replace writes (`updateUserMetadata` with no preceding read) do NOT need it.

## CRITICAL: lock-ordering invariant (deadlock avoidance)
There are TWO locks held during refinement persistence:
- `_refineLock` (in `UserDataHandler`) — acquired by the CALLER `_runRefinement` / `_dtCronJob`; serializes refinement-vs-refinement.
- `chatUserMetadataLock` — serializes refinement-vs-handler-metadata-writes.

Consistent ordering MUST be `_refineLock` (outer) → `chatUserMetadataLock` (inner). `_persistMemoryEntry` itself acquires ONLY `chatUserMetadataLock` (the outer `_refineLock` is already held by the caller). `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` acquires only `chatUserMetadataLock` (no `_refineLock`). No code path acquires them in reverse order — this MUST be preserved when touching either lock. Acquiring `chatUserMetadataLock` outer and `_refineLock` inner would deadlock.

## Verification note
The lock is `asyncio.Lock` (not `threading.RLock`, which the older `self.lock`/`_lock` use) because the read and write are `await` points on a single event loop — a threading lock cannot serialize across `await` yields. Full suite green: 2905 passed, 11 skipped.

title: Gotcha: wrapping handler code in async-with-cache-lock breaks plain-Mock cache fixtures — wire no-op CM
content:
Reusable testing gotcha, surfaced when adding `chatUserMetadataLock` to `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)`. Relates to (and partly carries out the "future test work" note in) memory `fa79a21f`, and complements the general async-CM mocking pattern in `13598eb2`.

## Symptom
After wrapping production handler code in `async with self.cache.someLockMethod():`, any test that installs a BARE `unittest.mock.Mock()` (or a Mock with only `AsyncMock` async-methods) as the handler's `self.cache` fails with:

`TypeError: 'unittest.mock.Mock' object does not support the asynchronous context manager protocol`

Calling `mock.someLockMethod()` returns a plain `Mock`, and `async with Mock():` raises because plain `Mock` has no real `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`.

## Why it bites
In this repo, several handler tests build a per-test mock cache via a helper rather than using a spec'd `AsyncMock`. `AsyncMock` DOES support async CM protocol, but a plain `Mock` does not, and a Mock whose attributes are individually set to `AsyncMock` only covers methods called+awaited — NOT methods that return an async context manager.

## Fix pattern (applied)
In `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_message_preprocessor.py`, the `_wireCacheForChatMember` helper now installs a real no-op async context manager stand-in:

```python
@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def _noopChatUserMetadataLock() -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    """No-op stand-in for ``CacheService.chatUserMetadataLock`` in tests."""
    yield

# inside the helper:
cache.chatUserMetadataLock = _noopChatUserMetadataLock
```

This is clearer and less fragile than configuring `__aenter__.return_value` on a Mock for a context-manager-returning METHOD (the pattern in `13598eb2` is better suited to mocking the CM object directly, e.g. `httpx.AsyncClient`).

## Rule of thumb
When you add any new `async with self.cache.X():` (or `self.db.X()`, `self.service.X()`) to production code, grep the test helpers that build a mock for that collaborator and wire `X` to a no-op async CM (or switch to a spec'd `AsyncMock`). A bare `Mock()` only happens to work for the methods currently called+awaited; adding a CM-returning call will break it.

title: Pyright: @contextlib.asynccontextmanager functions must be typed -> AsyncIterator[None], not -> Any
content:
Specific pyright (basic mode) rule, hit while adding `CacheService.chatUserMetadataLock`. Not covered by existing pyright-mock/union-narrowing memories.

## Symptom
A function decorated with `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` that does a bare `yield` (no value) and is annotated `-> Any` (or left without an async-generator return annotation) triggers:

`No overloads for "asynccontextmanager" match the provided arguments`
`Argument of type "() -> CoroutineType[Any, Any, Any]" cannot be assigned to parameter "func" of type "(**_P@asynccontextmanager) -> AsyncIterator[_T_co@asynccontextmanager]"`

## Cause
`@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` expects its target to be an async generator function (`AsyncIterator[T]`). With `-> Any` on an `async def ... yield`, pyright infers the function as returning a coroutine (`Coroutine[Any,Any,Any]`) rather than an async generator, so the decorator's overload doesn't match.

## Fix
Annotate the return type as `AsyncIterator[None]` (import from `typing` or `collections.abc`) for a value-less yield:

```python
from typing import AsyncIterator
import contextlib

@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def myLock() -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    """..."""
    yield
```

For a yield-with-value use `AsyncIterator[T]` with the concrete `T`. This is the repo-conforming way to declare an async context manager (no `# type: ignore` needed).

title: User memory refinement: >128-burst message-loss bugs ACCEPTED AS RISK (warning log added, NOT fixed)
content:
SUPersedes memory `ea8b2739` (which documents these bugs as "identified-unfixed" with reviewer-suggested fixes). As of the post-review fix round (2026-07-05), the user TRIAGED the >128-burst findings and deliberately ACCEPTED the risks instead of applying the fixes. These are no longer open bugs to fix — do NOT re-litigate or re-investigate unless requirements change.

## What was accepted as risk (unchanged from ea8b2739)
- **Bug 1**: `_dtCronJob` finally-block decrements `self._accounting[key]` by `preCount` (raw lifetime counter), not by messages-actually-processed. After a 200-msg burst: processes newest 128, subtracts 200, accounting zeroes, key dropped.
- **Bug 2**: `_runRefinement` advances cursor (`lastProcessedMessageDate`) to `messages[0]` (NEWEST of the newest-first batch). After a partial batch the cursor jumps past ALL messages including the unprocessed-older overflow; `getChatMessagesSince` only goes forward, so those older messages are permanently unreachable.

Both trigger when a single user sends >128 messages (`_memoryMaxMessagesPerRun`) between refinement ticks.

## Mitigation added instead of a fix: warning log
`internal/bot/common/handlers/user_data.py:514-522`. A `logger.warning` fires when `len(messages) >= self._memoryMaxMessagesPerRun` — the overflow-detection condition.
- **Condition is `>=`, not `>`**: with `limit=128`, the fetch returns AT MOST 128, so exactly 128 returned means the cap may have suppressed older rows.
- **Placement**: AFTER the `< minMessages` early-bail check (which returns before logging), so legit small batches don't warn.
- The warning message names the accepted-risk consequence ("older overflow messages will be skipped") and links the plan doc (`docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md`).

## Also accepted-as-risk (same finally block)
On `_runRefinement` EXCEPTION, accounting is STILL decremented by preCount. A persistent LLM outage zeroes every active user's credit each tick; recovery only via 5-more-messages or the 6h time threshold. Acceptable as accidental backoff.

## Gate 1 review verdict
The post-review fix round (lock race fix + warning log + docstring/typo fixes) was reviewed (2026-07-05) and found CLEAN — no Critical/Important issues. The `chatUserMetadataLock` implementation (memory 2e790f13) verified correct: lock held across full RMW in both callers, `_refineLock`→`chatUserMetadataLock` ordering consistent, `isUpdate=False` correctly outside lock. Two cosmetic recommendations only: add `-> AsyncIterator[None]` return hint on `chatUserMetadataLock` (see pyright rule memory 0c90c0b2), and one-line docstring note on the lock's intentionally-coarse global granularity.

title: No-op async-CM test wiring makes tests pass without asserting lock acquisition — coverage gap
content:
Known limitation of the no-op async-context-manager test-wiring pattern documented in memory `b5874b9c`. Surfaced and confirmed during the Gate 2 whole-work review of the `chatUserMetadataLock` fix round (2026-07-05).

## The gap
`_wireCacheForChatMember` in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_message_preprocessor.py` installs `_noopMetadataLock` (a `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` that just `yield`s) so that production code doing `async with self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock():` doesn't crash against a bare Mock. This makes the join/leave tests PASS — but nothing ASSERTS that `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` actually acquires the lock.

If a future change removes the `async with self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock():` wrapper from `setUserMetadata` (base.py) or `_persistMemoryEntry` (user_data.py), every test still passes: the no-op CM is installed on the mock but never entered. Same situation for `_persistMemoryEntry`'s tests in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_user_data.py` — they use a real `CacheService.getInstance()` (so the lock method is real), but again the acquisition is unasserted.

This is the "test passes whether or not the helper did the right thing" anti-pattern (memory `77cbfd08`), and it is in tension with the repo's hard regression-test mandate (memory `bf9348e3`). The lock is the entire point of the fix round, so silent regression is high-impact.

## Fix pattern (not yet applied — flagged as follow-up)
Add ONE focused test that uses a side-effect-tracking async-CM stand-in: an `acquired: bool` flag flipped on `__aenter__`, reset on `__aexit__`, then assert it was entered exactly once during a `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` call. Mirror the convention from the spam micro-opt tests (assert on the mock reference, not on `handler.cache`).

## General rule
Whenever you wire a no-op async CM into a mock collaborator to satisfy an `async with self.X.Y():` call site, you have made the test INSENSITIVE to whether Y is actually called. If the lock/acquire is the contract being tested, a no-op CM is insufficient by itself — pair it with a behavioural assertion that the CM was actually entered.

title: chatUserMetadataLock acquisition now asserted — no-op-CM coverage gap closed (5ffd2702 fixed)
content:
Resolves the coverage gap documented in memory `5ffd2702` (was status "identified-unfixed"). As of 2026-07-05, the `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` lock acquisition is now ASSERTED by regression tests, so silently removing the `async with self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock():` wrapper (memory `2e790f13`) makes a test fail.

## What was added
`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_base.py` — the dedicated `BaseBotHandler` test file (uses `UserDataHandler` as the concrete subclass via the `_makeHandler` helper, which resets the CacheService singleton and wires a real in-memory DB) — gained:
- A module-level `_CountingMetadataLock` class: an async-CM stand-in with an `enterCount: int` field incremented on `__aenter__`; `__aexit__` returns `False` (no exception suppression). Typed per repo convention: `Optional[type[BaseException]]`, `Optional[BaseException]`, `Optional[types.TracebackType]`.
- A new `TestSetUserMetadataLockContract` class with two tests:
  - `test_setUserMetadata_isUpdate_acquiresMetadataLock` — asserts `enterCount == 1` after `setUserMetadata(..., isUpdate=True)`, AND that `updateUserMetadata` received the shallow-merged dict `{**existing, **new}` (proves the RMW happened inside the lock).
  - `test_setUserMetadata_fullReplace_doesNotAcquireMetadataLock` — asserts `enterCount == 0` and `getUserMetadata` never called for `isUpdate=False` (pins that full-replace writes stay OUTSIDE the lock — no read, no race).

## Pattern (reusable for asserting any `async with self.cache.X():` contract)
Build the handler via `_makeHandler(testDatabase)`, then SWAP its cache:
```python
handler = await _makeHandler(testDatabase)
countingLock = _CountingMetadataLock()
cache = Mock()
cache.chatUserMetadataLock = Mock(return_value=countingLock)
cache.getUserMetadata = AsyncMock(return_value=cast(UserMetadataDict, {...}))
cache.updateUserMetadata = AsyncMock(return_value=None)
handler.cache = cache  # type: ignore[assignment]
```
See the companion convention memory for why `self.cache` is reassignable and why the `cast`/type-ignore are needed. This is the side-effect-tracking async-CM pattern `5ffd2702` recommended.

## Regression verified (do-not-skip-on-future-similar-work)
Commenting out the `async with self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock():` wrapper in `setUserMetadata` (base.py), dedenting the read-merge-write body so only the lock is removed, makes `test_setUserMetadata_isUpdate_acquiresMetadataLock` FAIL with `assert 0 == 1`; the `isUpdate=False` test still passes. Restoring the wrapper makes both pass. This closes the `77cbfd08`-style "test passes whether or not the helper did the right thing" anti-pattern.

## Also done in the same round (doc/comment follow-ups)
- `base.py` `setUserMetadata` docstring `Note:` section now states the `isUpdate=True` read-merge-write is serialized via `cache.chatUserMetadataLock()`. (Note: the instruction "don't restructure" left "When ``isUpdate=True``" appearing twice in the Note block — acceptable, reads as two distinct clauses.)
- `user_data.py` `_accountingLock` comment now notes the `_dtCronJob` scan-loop snapshot `list(self._accounting.items())` (~line 345) is intentionally taken WITHOUT the lock — `dict.items()` is atomic w.r.t. `await` on a single event loop. REUSABLE REASONING: an unlocked `dict.items()` snapshot is safe in single-event-loop async code as long as no `await` occurs between taking the snapshot and finishing its use; the lock guards the in-place mutate/subtract/drop sites, not the read-only snapshot.

Full suite green: 2907 passed, 11 skipped. `make format lint` clean (black collapsed the multi-line `AsyncMock(...)` onto one line).

title: Test conventions: reassigning handler.cache, cast for TypedDict literals, camelCase dunder params
content:
Reusable test-authoring typing conventions confirmed while writing the `chatUserMetadataLock` regression tests (2026-07-05). None were previously recorded; all cost lookup time.

## 1. Reassigning `handler.cache` (and other instance attrs) in tests
`BaseBotHandler.__init__` does `self.cache = CacheService.getInstance()` — a PLAIN instance attribute (not a property). So a test can build a real handler via `_makeHandler` and then SWAP the cache for a mock WITHOUT patching `getInstance`:
```python
handler = await _makeHandler(testDatabase)
handler.cache = cache  # type: ignore[assignment]
```
`# type: ignore[assignment]` is required (pyright sees `handler.cache: CacheService`; assigning a `Mock` is a mismatch). This matches the repo's existing `# type: ignore[…]` convention for test-time mock swaps (`test_message_preprocessor.py` uses `[method-assign]` for replacing a method, `[attr-defined]` for attribute access). Use `[assignment]` for reassigning a non-method instance attribute. Prefer this over `cast(CacheService, mock)` (an unchecked lie) or `cast(Any, ...)` (banned-ish).

## 2. `cast(UserMetadataDict, {...})` for TypedDict-typed params in tests
`UserMetadataDict` (`internal/bot/models/user_metadata.py`) is `TypedDict(total=False)` with DECLARED keys (`isSpammer`, `notSpammer`, `dropMessages`, `leftChat`). Pyright in basic mode structurally-checks dict literals passed to a `UserMetadataDict`-typed param, so a literal with UNDECLARED keys (e.g. `{"newKey": "newVal"}`) is REJECTED. Wrap test literals: `cast(UserMetadataDict, {"newKey": "newVal"})` (mirrors `tests/services/cache/test_user_info.py`). A plain dict is fine inside `AsyncMock(return_value={...})` because AsyncMock return values are loosely typed.

## 3. camelCase for `__aexit__` params — even dunders
The repo rule "camelCase for args" applies to `__aexit__` too: use `excType`, `exc`, `tb` — NOT `exc_type`. NOTE: existing code `internal/database/providers/base.py:260` uses snake_case `exc_type` (a PRE-EXISTING rule violation) — do not copy it. Full signature for a class-based async CM in this repo:
```python
async def __aexit__(
    self,
    excType: Optional[type[BaseException]],
    exc: Optional[BaseException],
    tb: Optional[types.TracebackType],
) -> bool:
```
(`import types`; `from typing import Optional`.) Param names are unconstrained for the `async with` protocol — pyright checks the shape (param count/types + return type), not names — so camelCase is safe and rule-compliant. `__init__`, `__aenter__` need docstrings per the "every method" rule even on tiny test helpers.

title: @asynccontextmanager factory methods: mock with Mock() not AsyncMock(), plus counting-CM assertion pattern
content:
Complements memory b5874b9c (which covers the bare-Mock failure + no-op `@asynccontextmanager` stand-in fix). Surfaces two insights NOT in b5874b9c, both observed in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_base.py::TestSetUserMetadataLockContract`.

## Insight 1: Mock the FACTORY with Mock(), never AsyncMock()

`chatUserMetadataLock` (internal/services/cache/service.py:1099) is `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager`-decorated. Decoration makes the CALL SYNCHRONOUS: `self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock()` returns an async context manager object (the CM, not a coroutine). The `async with` then drives it via `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`.

Trap: because the method is `async def`-shaped, a developer instinctively reaches for `AsyncMock(return_value=countingLock)`. That is WRONG — AsyncMock makes the factory call return a COROUTINE, so `async with self.cache.chatUserMetadataLock():` tries to use a coroutine as an async CM and fails. The factory call itself is not awaited.

Correct: `mockCache.chatUserMetadataLock = Mock(return_value=countingLock)` — a plain (synchronous) Mock so the call returns the CM object directly. `countingLock` is a real class implementing `__aenter__`/`__aexit__`.

Generalises to ANY `@asynccontextmanager`-decorated method (factory-call synchronous, CM is what's async). Applies to the sandbox docker backend and other async-CM usages in the repo too.

## Insight 2: Two distinct test patterns for async-CM-returning methods

Pattern A — **no-op pass-through** (from b5874b9c): use a real `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` no-op stand-in when you only need the `async with` to not crash and DON'T care whether the lock was taken.

Pattern B — **counting/asserting CM** (this conversation, TestSetUserMetadataLockContract): build an explicit helper class implementing `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` that increments `enterCount`, then assert `countingLock.enterCount == 0` (lock NOT taken on the `isUpdate=False` full-replace path) or `== 1` (lock taken on the `isUpdate=True` read-modify-write path). Use when the test's PURPOSE is to pin the locking contract, not just to pass through.

## Contract being pinned (for reference)
`setUserMetadata` (internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1083): `isUpdate=True` → acquire lock, read `getUserMetadata`, shallow-merge `{**existing, **metadata}`, write; `isUpdate=False` → write verbatim, NO lock, NO read. The `assert_not_called()` on `mockCache.getUserMetadata` in the `isUpdate=False` test guards against a speculative read regressing in.

title: userSummary injection simplified — moved into EnsuredMessage.setUserMetadata
content:
SUPERSEDES parts 2 & 3 of memory ddd8c864 (Phase 5 implementation). As of 2026-07-05, a simplification refactor changed how the memory-refinement summary is attached to messages. Branch `memory-refinement`, uncommitted as of the review.

## What changed (OLD → NEW)

**OLD (as ddd8c864 describes):**
- `BaseBotHandler.getUserMemorySummary(chatId, userId, threadId)` helper did the extraction: `cache.getUserMetadata` → `parseUserMetadata` → `memoryRefinement[str(threadId)]["summary"]`.
- Two injection sites, BOTH gated on the `MEMORY_REFINEMENT_ENABLED` chat setting:
  - `BaseBotHandler._updateEMessageUserData` (base.py) — checked the setting, then `ensuredMessage.userSummary = await self.getUserMemorySummary(...)`.
  - `HandlersManager._processMessageRec` (manager.py) — same gated attachment, reached the helper via `handlerObj = self.handlers[0][0]` (since HandlersManager isn't a BaseBotHandler subclass).
- Direct attribute assignment: `ensuredMessage.userSummary = ...`.

**NEW:**
- `BaseBotHandler.getUserMemorySummary` is DELETED. The `self.handlers[0][0]` routing for this purpose is gone from manager.py.
- Both injection sites now just do: `ensuredMessage.setUserMetadata(await self.cache.getUserMetadata(chatId=..., userId=...))`.
- New method `EnsuredMessage.setUserMetadata(metadata: UserMetadataDict) -> None` (internal/bot/models/ensured_message.py) owns the extraction: reads `self.threadId` (falling back to `dbUtils.DEFAULT_THREAD_ID`), looks up `metadata.get("memoryRefinement", {}).get(str(threadId), {}).get("summary")`, sets `self.userSummary` if non-empty. Leaves `userSummary=None` when absent.
- `DEFAULT_THREAD_ID` import removed from base.py and manager.py (no longer used there; still used inside ensured_message.py via dbUtils).
- `ChatSettingsKey`/`ChatSettingsValue` imports retained in both files (used elsewhere).

## BEHAVIOR CHANGE — gate removed at injection (gotcha)

The OLD code suppressed `userSummary` injection when `MEMORY_REFINEMENT_ENABLED` was false, even if stale summary data sat in `chat_users.metadata`. The NEW code injects whatever is in metadata unconditionally. In practice summaries are only WRITTEN when refinement is on (the write side in UserDataHandler still gates), so the only divergence is the "feature-disabled-but-stale-metadata" edge case: a chat that had refinement on, wrote summaries, then got disabled will now still inject the stale summary (previously suppressed). This is almost certainly the intended simplification but is undocumented in ADR-014 / the method docstring.

## Extraction correctness
`str(self.threadId or dbUtils.DEFAULT_THREAD_ID)` normalizes None → "0", matching how `_persistMemoryEntry` keys the entry (`str(threadId)`). The `if summary:` guard leaves the default None in place for absent/empty summaries, preserving the byte-identical-default-JSON invariant (omitted from formatForLLM output when None).

## Canonical docs / drift to fix
The simplification leaves these describing the OLD architecture:
- `docs/llm/memories/user-memory-refinement.md` (lines ~41, 56, 57, 90)
- `docs/llm/architecture.md` ADR-014 (~line 495)
- `docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md` and `docs/plans/user-info-cache-plan-v1.md` (historical; reference getUserMemorySummary)
Tests calling the deleted method: `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_base.py` (class TestGetUserMemorySummary — 4 cases) and `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_user_info_cache_regression.py` (lines ~232, ~302). These break at runtime; the 4 extraction cases belong on `EnsuredMessage.setUserMetadata` now (tests/bot/models/test_ensured_message.py).

title: Two setUserMetadata methods with opposite semantics (naming collision)
content:
After the 2026-07-05 userSummary-injection refactor, there are now TWO methods named `setUserMetadata` with OPPOSITE semantics — a real confusion risk:

1. `BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata(chatId, userId, metadata: UserMetadataDict, isUpdate: bool = False) -> None` (internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py ~line 1077) — PERSISTS metadata to the database (full replace, or shallow top-level merge when isUpdate=True).

2. `EnsuredMessage.setUserMetadata(metadata: UserMetadataDict) -> None` (internal/bot/models/ensured_message.py) — READ-ONLY extraction only: pulls `memoryRefinement[str(threadId)].summary` into `self.userSummary`. Does NOT persist, does NOT store the metadata on the message, discards everything else.

Same name, opposite meaning (one writes-through to DB, one only reads-from and throws the rest away). The original plan (`docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md` §10, and memory ddd8c864) deliberately proposed `setUserSummary` precisely to avoid this, noting "Deliberately did NOT add a `setUserSummary` setter; attachment uses direct attribute assignment". The refactor reversed that decision.

RECOMMENDATION (raised in review, not yet applied): rename `EnsuredMessage.setUserMetadata` → `setUserSummary` (or `applyUserMetadata` / `attachUserSummary`) to remove the ambiguity. If touched, also fix the new method's docstring — it currently says "Set user metadata for this message" which is misleading (nothing is stored on the message; only userSummary is set).
